children.title: Basis Matrix Representation

knowledge_statements.title: Basis Matrix Representation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Ordered-column definition for a standard-form linear program.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(A=[a_1\ \cdots\ a_n]\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\), and let \(\mathcal B=(j_1,\ldots,j_m)\) be an ordered tuple of distinct column indices. The basis matrix associated with \(\mathcal B\) is
\[
B:=A_{[:,\mathcal B]}=[a_{j_1}\ \cdots\ a_{j_m}]\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times m}.
\]
The ordering of \(\mathcal B\) fixes the ordering of columns in \(B\). The tuple \(\mathcal B\) is a simplex basis precisely when \(B\) is nonsingular.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A basis matrix consists of the constraint-matrix columns selected by an ordered set of m indices; those indices form a simplex basis exactly when the matrix is invertible.
assumptions_latex: A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}
\mathcal B=(j_1,\ldots,j_m)\text{ has distinct entries}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: B=A_{[:,\mathcal B]}=[a_{j_1}\ \cdots\ a_{j_m}],\quad \mathcal B\text{ is a basis}\iff \det(B)\ne0

notation.meaning: Ordered tuple of selected column indices.
Basis matrix induced by the selected indices.

children.title: Basis Column Set
children.top_down_role: Original-model columns selected for the current basis.

knowledge_statements.title: Basis Column Set
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unordered column-set view of a simplex basis.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(A=[a_1\ \cdots\ a_n]\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\) and an index set \(\mathcal B\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}\) with \(|\mathcal B|=m\), the selected basis-column set is
\[
\mathscr C_{\mathcal B}:=\{a_j:j\in\mathcal B\}.
\]
It is a basis column set when its vectors are linearly independent. Because it contains exactly \(m\) vectors in \(\mathbb R^m\), this is equivalent to \(\operatorname{span}(\mathscr C_{\mathcal B})=\mathbb R^m\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The basis column set contains the m columns indexed by the basic indices and is valid exactly when those columns are linearly independent, equivalently spanning the constraint space.
assumptions_latex: A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}
\mathcal B\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\},\quad |\mathcal B|=m
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathscr C_{\mathcal B}=\{a_j:j\in\mathcal B\},\quad \mathscr C_{\mathcal B}\text{ is a basis}\iff \operatorname{span}(\mathscr C_{\mathcal B})=\mathbb R^m

notation.meaning: Set of columns selected by the basic indices.

children.title: Column-to-Matrix Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Indexing correspondence between selected model columns plus basis-matrix positions.

knowledge_statements.title: Column-to-Matrix Correspondence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Correspondence between selected columns, index ordering, and the basis matrix.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\mathcal B=\{j_1,\ldots,j_m\}\) select \(m\) columns of \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\). Every ordering \((j_1,\ldots,j_m)\) represents the selected set by
\[
B=[a_{j_1}\ \cdots\ a_{j_m}].
\]
If another ordering produces \(\widetilde B\), then \(\widetilde B=BP\) for a permutation matrix \(P\). Consequently, rank and nonsingularity depend only on the selected column set, while coordinates such as \(x_{\mathcal B}\) must use the same ordering as \(B\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Ordering selected columns forms a basis matrix. Reordering only right-multiplies it by a permutation matrix, preserving rank and invertibility while permuting basic coordinates consistently.
assumptions_latex: A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}
\mathcal B=\{j_1,\ldots,j_m\}\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: B=[a_{j_1}\ \cdots\ a_{j_m}],\quad \widetilde B=BP,\quad \operatorname{rank}(\widetilde B)=\operatorname{rank}(B)

notation.meaning: Matrix formed from one ordering of the selected columns.
Basic-coordinate vector ordered consistently with B.

children.title: Basic Index Set
children.top_down_role: Indices currently assigned to basis membership.

knowledge_statements.title: Basic Index Set
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Index-set definition for a simplex basis in standard form.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) have row rank \(m\). A basic index set is a subset \(\mathcal B\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}\) satisfying \(|\mathcal B|=m\) such that the submatrix \(A_{[:,\mathcal B]}\) is nonsingular. Its elements label the basic variables and the columns used to solve the equality system. An ordering of \(\mathcal B\) is chosen whenever basic-variable coordinates or the basis matrix are written as vectors or matrices.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A basic index set contains m indices whose corresponding columns form an invertible square matrix; its indices label the basic variables.
assumptions_latex: A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}
\operatorname{rank}(A)=m
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathcal B\text{ is basic}\iff |\mathcal B|=m\ \text{and}\ \det(A_{[:,\mathcal B]})\ne0

notation.meaning: Submatrix containing columns indexed by the basic set.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Dual simplex pivot preserving dual feasibility
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One pivot of the dual simplex method for a standard-form linear program, including its optimality test and the condition under which the ratio step is defined.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(\min\{c^Tx:Ax=b,\ x\ge 0\}\) and its dual \(\max\{b^T\lambda:A^T\lambda+s=c,\ s\ge0\}\). Let \(A=[B\ N]\) with \(B\) nonsingular, and set \(x_B=B^{-1}b\), \(x_N=0\), \(\lambda=B^{-T}c_B\), \(s_B=0\), and \(s_N=c_N-N^T\lambda\ge0\). If \(x_B\ge0\), then \((x,\lambda,s)\) is primal-dual optimal. Otherwise choose \(q\in\mathcal B\) with \(x_q<0\), solve \(B^Tv=-e_q\), and put \(w=N^Tv\). Provided \(\{j\in\mathcal N:w_j>0\}\neq\varnothing\), choose \(\alpha=\min_{j\in\mathcal N,\,w_j>0}s_j/w_j\) and an attaining index \(r\). Update \(\lambda^+=\lambda+\alpha v\) and \(s_N^+=s_N-\alpha w\), so \(s^+\ge0\) and \(s_r^+=0\). Solve \(Bd=A_r\), set \(\gamma=x_q/d_q\), and update \(x_i^+=x_i-\gamma d_i\) for \(i\in\mathcal B\setminus\{q\}\), \(x_q^+=0\), \(x_r^+=\gamma\), and all other nonbasic components to zero. Since \(d_q=-w_r<0\), \(\gamma>0\); exchanging \(q\) and \(r\) preserves \(Ax^+=b\), dual feasibility, and complementarity while moving the iteration toward primal feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a standard-form linear program, start from a nonsingular basic/nonbasic column partition whose associated point is dual feasible and complementary, although its basic primal variables may be negative. If all basic primal variables are nonnegative, the current primal-dual point is optimal. Otherwise select a negative basic component, compute the dual direction, and—when at least one positive ratio denominator exists—use the minimum-ratio test to choose an entering nonbasic column without losing dual feasibility. The corresponding primal update makes the leaving component zero, makes the entering component positive, preserves the equality constraints and complementarity, and exchanges the two indices.
assumptions_latex: \(A=[B\ N]\) with \(B\) nonsingular and index partition \(\mathcal B\cup\mathcal N\).
\(x_B=B^{-1}b,\ x_N=0,\ \lambda=B^{-T}c_B,\ s_B=0,\ s_N=c_N-N^T\lambda\ge0\).
If a pivot is required, \(q\in\mathcal B\) satisfies \(x_q<0\).
For the stated finite ratio step, \(\{j\in\mathcal N:(N^Tv)_j>0\}\neq\varnothing\), where \(B^Tv=-e_q\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Either \(x_B\ge0\) and \((x,\lambda,s)\) is optimal, or the stated ratio test and exchange \(q\leftrightarrow r\) produce an updated equality-feasible, dual-feasible, complementary simplex state with \(x_q^+=0\), \(s_r^+=0\), and \(x_r^+>0\).

children.title: Nonbasic Index Set
children.top_down_role: Indices currently assigned outside the basis.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonbasic Index Set
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Complementary index-set definition relative to a chosen basis.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a chosen basic index set \(\mathcal B\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}\), the associated nonbasic index set is
\[
\mathcal N:=\{1,\ldots,n\}\setminus\mathcal B.
\]
Thus \(\mathcal N\) contains exactly the indices not used in the basis matrix. When \(|\mathcal B|=m\), one has \(|\mathcal N|=n-m\). In the standard basic solution associated with \(\mathcal B\), variables indexed by \(\mathcal N\) are fixed at their lower bound zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The nonbasic index set is the complement of the basic indices. It has n−m elements, and its variables are zero in the associated standard-form basic solution.
assumptions_latex: \mathcal B\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}
|\mathcal B|=m
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathcal N=\{1,\ldots,n\}\setminus\mathcal B,\quad |\mathcal N|=n-m

children.title: Index-Partition Consistency
children.top_down_role: Coverage plus exclusivity conditions for the two index classes.

knowledge_statements.title: Index-Partition Consistency
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Consistency predicate for basic and nonbasic index collections relative to a valid simplex basis.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), let \(c,x\in\mathbb R^n\), and let \(\mathcal B,\mathcal N\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}\). The pair \((\mathcal B,\mathcal N)\) is a consistent basic–nonbasic partition when
\[
\mathcal B\cap\mathcal N=\varnothing,\qquad \mathcal B\cup\mathcal N=\{1,\ldots,n\},\qquad |\mathcal B|=m,
\]
and the selected matrix \(A_{[:,\mathcal B]}\) is nonsingular. After choosing orderings of \(\mathcal B\) and \(\mathcal N\), the vectors \(x_{\mathcal B}\) and \(c_{\mathcal B}\) must follow the ordering used in \(A_{[:,\mathcal B]}\), while \(x_{\mathcal N}\) and \(c_{\mathcal N}\) must follow the ordering used in \(A_{[:,\mathcal N]}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A consistent basic–nonbasic partition is disjoint and exhaustive, has m basic indices whose columns form a nonsingular matrix, and uses consistent index orderings in all associated matrices and vectors.
assumptions_latex: A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}
c,x\in\mathbb R^n
\mathcal B,\mathcal N\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathcal B\cap\mathcal N=\varnothing,\quad \mathcal B\cup\mathcal N=\{1,\ldots,n\},\quad |\mathcal B|=m,\quad \det(A_{[:,\mathcal B]})\ne0

notation.meaning: Nonbasic index set complementary to the basic set.
Columns of A ordered according to the chosen ordering of the basic indices.

children.title: Nonsingular Basis Regime
children.top_down_role: Full-rank basis states suitable for basis solves.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonsingular Basis Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact rank-regularity condition for a valid simplex basis.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) and \(\mathcal B\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}\) with \(|\mathcal B|=m\), write \(B=A_{[:,\mathcal B]}\). The selection lies in the nonsingular basis regime exactly when
\[
\operatorname{rank}(B)=m,
\]
equivalently \(\det(B)\ne0\) or the smallest singular value satisfies \(\sigma_{\min}(B)>0\). In this regime, for every \(b\in\mathbb R^m\), the basic equation \(Bx_{\mathcal B}=b\) has the unique solution \(x_{\mathcal B}=B^{-1}b\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A selected square column matrix is a valid basis exactly when it has full rank, equivalently nonzero determinant or positive smallest singular value; then every basic system has a unique solution.
assumptions_latex: A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}
\mathcal B\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\},\quad |\mathcal B|=m
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{rank}(B)=m\iff \det(B)\ne0\iff \sigma_{\min}(B)>0

children.title: Rank-Deficient Column Selection
children.top_down_role: Selected-column states that fail the basis rank requirement.

knowledge_statements.title: Rank-Deficient Column Selection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Algebraic failure caused by selecting dependent candidate basis columns.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(B=A_{[:,\mathcal B]}\in\mathbb R^{m\times m}\) be formed from \(m\) selected columns. If \(\operatorname{rank}(B)<m\), then the selection is not a simplex basis: \(B^{-1}\) does not exist. For a right-hand side \(b\in\mathbb R^m\), the equation \(Bx_{\mathcal B}=b\) is inconsistent when \(b\notin\operatorname{range}(B)\), and has infinitely many solutions when \(b\in\operatorname{range}(B)\). Hence it never determines a unique basic-variable state.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dependent selected columns do not form a basis. The basic system is either inconsistent or nonunique, so no unique basic-variable state can be computed.
assumptions_latex: B=A_{[:,\mathcal B]}\in\mathbb R^{m\times m}
\operatorname{rank}(B)<m
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: B^{-1}\text{ does not exist, and }Bx_{\mathcal B}=b\text{ has either zero or infinitely many solutions}

children.title: Near-Rank-Loss Boundary
children.top_down_role: Basis states approaching numerical rank loss.

knowledge_statements.title: Near-Rank-Loss Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Numerical boundary where a nonsingular basis approaches singularity under spectral-norm normalization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every nonsingular \(B\in\mathbb R^{m\times m}\), its spectral-norm distance to the set of singular matrices is
\[
\operatorname{dist}_2\bigl(B,\{S\in\mathbb R^{m\times m}:\det(S)=0\}\bigr)=\sigma_{\min}(B),
\]
and its spectral-norm condition number is
\[
\kappa_2(B)=\frac{\sigma_{\max}(B)}{\sigma_{\min}(B)}.
\]
Consequently, for a sequence of nonsingular matrices \((B_k)\) normalized by \(\sigma_{\max}(B_k)=1\), if \(\sigma_{\min}(B_k)\to0\), then the distance to singularity tends to zero and \(\kappa_2(B_k)\to\infty\). Thus solving \(B_kx_{\mathcal B}=b\), with \(b\in\mathbb R^m\), becomes increasingly sensitive to relative perturbations although every \(B_k\) remains invertible.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a spectrally normalized sequence of nonsingular basis matrices, approaching rank loss means that the smallest singular value and distance to singularity tend to zero; the condition number then diverges and basic-system solutions become increasingly perturbation-sensitive.
assumptions_latex: B_k\in\mathbb R^{m\times m}\text{ is nonsingular for every }k
\sigma_{\max}(B_k)=1
\sigma_{\min}(B_k)\to0
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{dist}_2(B_k,\{S\in\mathbb R^{m\times m}:\det(S)=0\})\to0,\quad \kappa_2(B_k)\to\infty

notation.meaning: Distance induced by the spectral matrix norm.

knowledge_statements.title: Basic-Variable State
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Basic-coordinate component of a standard-form basic solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Consider the standard-form constraints \(Ax=b\) with a basic–nonbasic partition \((\mathcal B,\mathcal N)\). Let \(B=A_{[:,\mathcal B]}\) be nonsingular and \(N=A_{[:,\mathcal N]}\). The equality system is
\[
Bx_{\mathcal B}+Nx_{\mathcal N}=b.
\]
After assigning the nonbasic state \(x_{\mathcal N}=0\), the basic-variable state is uniquely
\[
x_{\mathcal B}=B^{-1}b.
\]
Its components are ordered consistently with the columns of \(B\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With nonbasic variables set to zero, the basic-variable state is the unique solution B⁻¹b, ordered consistently with the basis columns.
assumptions_latex: Ax=b,\quad A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}
B=A_{[:,\mathcal B]}\text{ is nonsingular}
x_{\mathcal N}=0
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x_{\mathcal B}=B^{-1}b

knowledge_statements.title: Nonbasic-Variable State
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonbasic-coordinate component of a standard-form basic solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a standard-form linear program with \(x\ge0\) and a chosen basic–nonbasic partition \((\mathcal B,\mathcal N)\), the nonbasic-variable state of the associated basic solution is defined by
\[
x_j=0\quad\text{for every }j\in\mathcal N,
\]
or equivalently \(x_{\mathcal N}=0\in\mathbb R^{n-m}\). This assignment fixes all nonbasic coordinates at their lower bounds and reduces \(Ax=b\) to the square basic system \(Bx_{\mathcal B}=b\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In a standard-form basic solution, every nonbasic variable is fixed at zero, reducing the equality constraints to the square system for the basic variables.
assumptions_latex: x\in\mathbb R^n_{+}
(\mathcal B,\mathcal N)\text{ is a basic–nonbasic partition}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x_{\mathcal N}=0\in\mathbb R^{n-m}

knowledge_statements.title: Basic Feasibility State
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Feasibility test for a standard-form basic solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For the standard-form constraints \(Ax=b\), \(x\ge0\), let \(B=A_{[:,\mathcal B]}\) be nonsingular and define the associated basic solution by \(x_{\mathcal B}=B^{-1}b\) and \(x_{\mathcal N}=0\). This basic solution is feasible if and only if
\[
B^{-1}b\ge0
\]
componentwise. Equality in one or more components is permitted; the resulting feasible basis is degenerate when at least one basic component equals zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A standard-form basic solution is feasible exactly when B⁻¹b is componentwise nonnegative; it is degenerate if any resulting basic variable is zero.
assumptions_latex: Ax=b,\quad x\ge0
B=A_{[:,\mathcal B]}\text{ is nonsingular}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x\text{ is a basic feasible solution}\iff B^{-1}b\ge0

children.title: Nonbasic Lower-Bound Status
children.top_down_role: Nonbasic-variable state associated with an active lower bound.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonbasic Lower-Bound Status
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the conventional bounded-variable simplex status partition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A nonbasic index \(j\in N\) has lower-bound status precisely when its lower bound is finite and its basis-state value equals that bound: \(\ell_j\in\mathbb{R}\) and \(x_j=\ell_j\). Such indices form \(N_L:=\{j\in N:\ell_j\in\mathbb{R},\ x_j=\ell_j\}\). Given all nonbasic values, the associated basic vector is determined by \(x_B=A_B^{-1}(b-A_Nx_N)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonbasic variable has lower-bound status when it is fixed at its finite lower bound; the basic variables are then recovered from the equality constraints.
assumptions_latex: The bounded-form linear program is \(Ax=b\) with \(\ell\le x\le u\), where \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\) has rank \(m\).
A basis index set \(B\) has \(|B|=m\) and nonsingular \(A_B\); its complement is \(N\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(j\in N_L\iff \ell_j\in\mathbb{R}\text{ and }x_j=\ell_j\).

notation.meaning: Indices of nonbasic variables assigned to finite lower bounds

children.title: Opposite-Bound Status Transition
children.top_down_role: Changes between the two nonbasic bound statuses.

assumptions_latex: A feasible bounded-variable basis state has \(j\in N_L\), finite bounds \(\ell_j<u_j\), and basis matrix \(A_B\).
The full displacement \(\Delta=u_j-\ell_j\) preserves every basic-variable bound along \(x_B(t)=x_B-A_B^{-1}a_jt\) for \(0\le t\le\Delta\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_j:\ell_j\mapsto u_j\), \(x_B\mapsto x_B-A_B^{-1}a_j(u_j-\ell_j)\), and \(j:N_L\mapsto N_U\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize \(t=0\) and increase \(x_j=\ell_j+t\), maintaining equality feasibility by \(x_B(t)=x_B-A_B^{-1}a_jt\). If no basic variable reaches a bound before \(t=\Delta:=u_j-\ell_j\), stop at \(t=\Delta\), retain \(B\), replace the lower-bound status of \(j\) by upper-bound status, and output the updated feasible basis state. The reverse transition uses \(t\) from \(u_j\) toward \(\ell_j\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Move a nonbasic variable completely to its opposite finite bound while compensating with basic variables; if feasibility persists, keep the basis and flip its status.

children.title: Free-Variable Status
children.top_down_role: Basis-state treatment of variables without finite bounds.

knowledge_statements.title: Free-Variable Status
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines freedom solely through the absence of finite bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A variable \(x_j\) has free-variable status when it has neither a finite lower bound nor a finite upper bound, namely \(\ell_j=-\infty\) and \(u_j=+\infty\). Its value is therefore unrestricted by bound constraints, although it remains subject to the linear equalities and any other constraints of the model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A variable is free when neither endpoint of its allowable interval is finite, although the model's linear constraints may still restrict its value.
assumptions_latex: Variable \(x_j\) belongs to a linear program with bounds \(\ell_j\le x_j\le u_j\), allowing infinite endpoints.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_j\text{ is free}\iff \ell_j=-\infty\text{ and }u_j=+\infty\).

children.title: Fixed-Variable Status
children.top_down_role: Basis-state treatment of variables whose bounds coincide.

assumptions_latex: Variable \(x_j\) belongs to a linear program with bounds \(\ell_j\le x_j\le u_j\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_j\text{ is fixed}\iff \ell_j=u_j\in\mathbb{R}\), in which case \(x_j=\ell_j\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A variable \(x_j\) has fixed-variable status when its lower and upper bounds coincide at a finite value: \(\ell_j=u_j=\gamma_j\in\mathbb{R}\). Every feasible point then satisfies \(x_j=\gamma_j\), so the variable has no feasible bound displacement and may be eliminated by substituting \(a_j\gamma_j\) into the equality right-hand side.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A variable is fixed when its finite lower and upper bounds coincide; every feasible solution must assign that common value.
knowledge_statements.title: Fixed-Variable Status

children.title: Status-Specific Basis Eligibility
children.top_down_role: Basis-membership implications associated with free or fixed status.

assumptions_latex: A bounded-variable simplex state represents \(Ax=b\), \(\ell\le x\le u\), using a nonsingular basis matrix \(A_B\).
The implementation requires every nonbasic variable to be assigned to one of its finite bounds.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(j\notin B\Rightarrow \ell_j\in\mathbb{R}\text{ or }u_j\in\mathbb{R}\); free variables require basic status, while fixed variables may be retained nonbasic at their common bound.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Eligibility is relative to a bound-status-only nonbasic representation.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under a basis-state convention in which every nonbasic variable must equal a finite bound, basis eligibility satisfies \(F\subseteq B\), where \(F:=\{j:\ell_j=-\infty,\ u_j=+\infty\}\). A fixed index \(j\in K:=\{j:\ell_j=u_j\in\mathbb{R}\}\) may instead be nonbasic at its common bound; retaining it in \(B\) is algebraically possible only when \(A_B\) remains nonsingular, but necessarily produces a zero-width, degenerate basic component.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With bound-assigned nonbasic variables, every free variable must be basic. A fixed variable may be nonbasic; if retained in a nonsingular basis, it is necessarily degenerate.
knowledge_statements.title: Status-Specific Basis Eligibility

knowledge_statements.title: Bound-Partition Feasibility State
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Represents feasibility for finite-bound nonbasic partitions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A bound-partition basis state is the partition \((B,N_L,N_U)\), where every \(j\in N_L\) has \(\ell_j\in\mathbb{R}\) and every \(j\in N_U\) has \(u_j\in\mathbb{R}\), together with \(x_{N_L}=\ell_{N_L}\), \(x_{N_U}=u_{N_U}\), and \[x_B=A_B^{-1}\bigl(b-A_{N_L}\ell_{N_L}-A_{N_U}u_{N_U}\bigr).\] It is primal feasible if and only if every basic component satisfies \(\ell_i\le (x_B)_i\le u_i\) for \(i\in B\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bound partition fixes each nonbasic variable at a designated finite bound, solves uniquely for the basic variables, and is feasible exactly when those basic values satisfy their bounds.
assumptions_latex: The system is \(Ax=b\), \(\ell\le x\le u\), with \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\) of rank \(m\).
The sets \(B,N_L,N_U\) partition \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\), with \(|B|=m\) and nonsingular \(A_B\).
For every \(j\in N_L\), \(\ell_j\in\mathbb{R}\), and for every \(j\in N_U\), \(u_j\in\mathbb{R}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_{N_L}=\ell_{N_L}\), \(x_{N_U}=u_{N_U}\), and \(x_B=A_B^{-1}(b-A_{N_L}\ell_{N_L}-A_{N_U}u_{N_U})\), with feasibility exactly when \(\ell_B\le x_B\le u_B\).

notation.meaning: Basic, lower-nonbasic, and upper-nonbasic index sets

knowledge_statements.title: Nondegenerate Basis–Vertex Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: States the one-to-one correspondence in the bounded-form nondegenerate regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In a nondegenerate bounded-variable basis state, every nonbasic index is active at exactly one finite bound and every basic index is strictly off each of its finite bounds. Hence exactly \(n-m\) bound constraints are active, all indexed by \(N\). Consequently the feasible basis state determines a vertex of \(P\), and the vertex's active bound constraints uniquely recover \(N\), their lower-or-upper statuses, and the complementary basis \(B\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When exactly the nonbasic variables are active at one bound each and all basic variables are strictly off their finite bounds, the feasible basis state and its vertex determine one another uniquely.
assumptions_latex: The feasible set is \(P=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:Ax=b,\ \ell\le x\le u\}\), where \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\) and \(\operatorname{rank}(A)=m\).
A feasible basis state has a set \(B\) with \(|B|=m\) and nonsingular \(A_B\), and its complement is \(N\).
For each \(j\in N\), the value \(x_j\) equals exactly one finite bound and differs strictly from the opposite bound whenever that opposite bound is finite.
For each \(i\in B\), \(x_i>\ell_i\) whenever \(\ell_i\in\mathbb{R}\), and \(x_i<u_i\) whenever \(u_i\in\mathbb{R}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The state determines a vertex having exactly \(n-m\) active bound constraints, and those active bounds uniquely determine the same nonbasic statuses and complementary basis.

notation.meaning: Basis and complementary nonbasis index sets

children.title: Degenerate Vertex Structure
children.top_down_role: Vertex-level geometry associated with excess active constraints.

assumptions_latex: The standard-form feasible set is \(P=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:Ax=b,\ x\ge0\}\), where \(A\) has rank \(m\).
A vertex \(x\) is represented by a feasible basis \(B\), so \(x_N=0\) and \(x_B=A_B^{-1}b\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\) is degenerate with respect to \(B\iff \exists i\in B\) such that \(x_i=0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the standard-form basic-feasible-solution definition of degeneracy.

source_refs.locator: 2. Two Examples of Degenerate Problems p. 27
Bases and Vertices p. 32

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The basic feasible solution associated with \(B\) is degenerate when at least one basic component vanishes: \(x_i=0\) for some \(i\in B\). Equivalently, more than the required \(n-m\) nonnegativity constraints are active at the represented vertex. The number \(|\{i\in B:x_i=0\}|\) is the basis-relative degree of degeneracy.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A standard-form basic feasible solution is degenerate when one or more basic variables are zero, so more nonnegativity constraints than necessary are active.
knowledge_statements.title: Degenerate Vertex Structure

source_witnesses.locator: 2. Two Examples of Degenerate Problems p. 27
Bases and Vertices p. 32

children.title: Multiple Bases per Vertex
children.top_down_role: Alternative basis states representing the same vertex.

assumptions_latex: The standard-form feasible set is \(P=\{x:Ax=b,\ x\ge0\}\), with \(\operatorname{rank}(A)=m\).
A vertex \(x\) has positive support \(S=\{j:x_j>0\}\) with \(|S|<m\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every \(B\supseteq S\) with \(|B|=m\) and nonsingular \(A_B\) represents the same vertex \(x\); distinct such sets are distinct bases for \(x\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes basis multiplicity at a standard-form degenerate vertex.

source_refs.locator: Bases and Vertices p. 32
2. Two Examples of Degenerate Problems p. 27

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a vertex \(x\), any index set \(B\) satisfying \(S\subseteq B\), \(|B|=m\), and \(A_B\) nonsingular represents \(x\): indices in \(B\setminus S\) are zero basic variables and every index outside \(B\) is nonbasic at zero. Thus, whenever two distinct nonsingular completions of \(S\) exist, the same degenerate vertex is represented by multiple bases.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A degenerate vertex can have several bases: each is a nonsingular completion of the vertex's positive support by indices whose variables remain zero.
knowledge_statements.title: Multiple Bases per Vertex

source_witnesses.locator: Bases and Vertices p. 32
2. Two Examples of Degenerate Problems p. 27

children.title: Vertex-Preserving Basis Exchange
children.top_down_role: Basis changes that retain the represented vertex.

assumptions_latex: A standard-form basic feasible solution \(x\) is represented by basis \(B\).
For some \(q\notin B\), the simplex direction has a leaving index \(p\in B\) whose ratio-test step is \(\theta=0\), and \(B'=(B\setminus\{p\})\cup\{q\}\) is nonsingular.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x'=x+\theta d=x\) and \(B'\ne B\); hence the pivot changes the basis but preserves the vertex.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Covers a zero-step simplex pivot at a degenerate vertex.

source_refs.locator: 2. Two Examples of Degenerate Problems p. 27
3.5 Algebra of the Simplex Method p. 108

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(d\) be the feasible simplex direction generated by entering index \(q\). If the minimum-ratio test selects a zero basic variable \(p\) and returns \(\theta=0\), then the pivot produces \(B'=(B\setminus\{p\})\cup\{q\}\) while the primal point satisfies \(x'=x+\theta d=x\). Provided \(A_{B'}\) is nonsingular, this is a vertex-preserving basis exchange.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In a degenerate zero-length pivot, one basic index is exchanged for an entering index, but the primal point and therefore the represented vertex do not move.
knowledge_statements.title: Vertex-Preserving Basis Exchange

source_witnesses.locator: 2. Two Examples of Degenerate Problems p. 27
3.5 Algebra of the Simplex Method p. 108

children.title: Basis Adjacency
children.top_down_role: Neighboring basis states under a single basis exchange.

assumptions_latex: Basis index sets \(B,B'\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}\) both have cardinality \(m\), and \(A_B\) and \(A_{B'}\) are nonsingular.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(B\sim B'\iff |B\setminus B'|=|B'\setminus B|=1\), equivalently \(|B\cap B'|=m-1\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines combinatorial adjacency in the basis-exchange graph.

source_refs.locator: 3.5 Algebra of the Simplex Method p. 108
Bases and Vertices p. 32

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Two bases \(B\) and \(B'\) are basis-adjacent when one valid basis exchange transforms one into the other. Formally, there exist unique indices \(p\in B\setminus B'\) and \(q\in B'\setminus B\) such that \(B'=(B\setminus\{p\})\cup\{q\}\). Equivalently, \(|B\cap B'|=m-1\). This definition concerns basis sets and does not require their represented feasible points to be distinct.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two nonsingular bases are adjacent when they differ by exactly one leaving index and one entering index, even if degeneracy makes them represent the same point.
knowledge_statements.title: Basis Adjacency

source_witnesses.locator: 3.5 Algebra of the Simplex Method p. 108
Bases and Vertices p. 32

children.title: Edge Adjacency
children.top_down_role: Neighboring vertices connected by a feasible polyhedral edge.

assumptions_latex: \(P=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:Ax=b,\ x\ge 0\}\) is nonempty.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(u\sim_E v\iff u\ne v\) and \([u,v]\) is a one-dimensional face of \(P\).

notation.meaning: Edge adjacency relation on vertices of the polyhedron.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Polyhedral edge adjacency for distinct basic feasible solutions in standard form.

source_refs.locator: 2. The Primal Simplex Method p. 91

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(u\) and \(v\) be vertices of \(P\). They are edge-adjacent, written \(u\sim_E v\), precisely when \(u\ne v\) and their convex hull \([u,v]=\{(1-t)u+tv:0\le t\le 1\}\) is a one-dimensional face of \(P\). Equivalently, there exists a supporting hyperplane \(H\) of \(P\) such that \(P\cap H=[u,v]\). Thus adjacency concerns a geometric edge, not merely two basis descriptions differing by one column.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two distinct vertices are edge-adjacent exactly when the segment joining them is a one-dimensional face of the feasible polyhedron.
knowledge_statements.title: Edge Adjacency

source_witnesses.locator: 2. The Primal Simplex Method p. 91

children.title: Adjacency Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Regimes where combinatorial neighbors align with geometric neighbors.

assumptions_latex: \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\) has rank \(m\), and \(P=\{x:Ax=b,\ x\ge0\}\).
Every basic feasible solution of \(P\) is nondegenerate: its \(m\) basic components are positive.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x(B)\sim_E x(B')\iff |B\setminus B'|=|B'\setminus B|=1\).

notation.meaning: A set of m indices whose columns form a nonsingular basis matrix.
The basic feasible solution associated with a basis.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nondegenerate basis-edge correspondence for a standard-form polyhedron.

source_refs.locator: 2. The Primal Simplex Method p. 91

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For feasible bases \(B\) and \(B'\), nondegeneracy makes the associated vertices \(x(B)\) and \(x(B')\) distinct whenever the bases are distinct. These vertices are joined by an edge of \(P\) if and only if their bases exchange exactly one column: \[x(B)\sim_E x(B')\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad |B\setminus B'|=|B'\setminus B|=1.\] Hence, under nondegeneracy, a simplex pivot between feasible bases corresponds exactly to traversal of a polyhedral edge.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In a nondegenerate standard-form polyhedron, two feasible bases differ by one column exactly when their vertices share an edge.
knowledge_statements.title: Adjacency Correspondence

source_witnesses.locator: 2. The Primal Simplex Method p. 91

children.title: Degenerate Adjacency Mismatch
children.top_down_role: Degenerate cases where the two adjacency notions diverge.

assumptions_latex: \(P=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^3:Ax=b,\ x\ge0\}\), where \(A=\begin{pmatrix}1&1&0\\0&1&1\end{pmatrix}\) and \(b=(1,1)^{\mathsf T}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(|B_1\setminus B_2|=|B_2\setminus B_1|=1\) but \(x(B_1)=x(B_2)=(0,1,0)^{\mathsf T}\), so basis adjacency does not imply edge adjacency.

notation.meaning: The basis consisting of columns one and two.
The basis consisting of columns two and three.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete degeneracy obstruction to identifying basis adjacency with geometric edge adjacency.

source_refs.locator: 2. The Primal Simplex Method p. 91

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Both \(B_1=\{1,2\}\) and \(B_2=\{2,3\}\) are nonsingular feasible bases, and they differ by one exchanged column. Nevertheless, solving the two basic systems gives \[x(B_1)=x(B_2)=(0,1,0)^{\mathsf T}.\] The common basic feasible solution is degenerate because one basic component is zero. Thus adjacent basis states may encode the same vertex and consequently no geometric edge traversal. The basis-edge adjacency equivalence therefore fails without nondegeneracy.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Degeneracy can make adjacent bases represent the same vertex, so a one-column basis exchange need not traverse a geometric edge.
knowledge_statements.title: Degenerate Adjacency Mismatch

source_witnesses.locator: 2. The Primal Simplex Method p. 91

assumptions_latex: The primal problem is \(\max\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax=b,\ x\ge0\}\), with \(A\) of row rank \(m\).
\(B\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}\) has size \(m\) and \(A_B\) is nonsingular.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(y_B=A_B^{-\mathsf T}c_B\), equivalently \(A_B^{\mathsf T}y_B=c_B\).

notation.meaning: The nonsingular matrix formed by basic columns.
The objective coefficients indexed by the basis.
The simplex multiplier associated with the basis.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Multiplier representation for a maximization problem in equality standard form.

source_refs.locator: 2. The Dual Simplex Method p. 152

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The simplex multiplier state induced by \(B\) is the unique vector \(y_B\in\mathbb{R}^m\) satisfying \[A_B^{\mathsf T}y_B=c_B,\qquad y_B=A_B^{-\mathsf T}c_B.\] It assigns dual prices to the equality constraints and makes every basic reduced cost vanish. The state depends only on the selected basis and its basic objective coefficients; it is defined whether or not the associated basic solution is primal feasible or the multiplier is dual feasible.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A basis determines a unique simplex multiplier by solving the transposed basis system against the basic objective coefficients.
knowledge_statements.title: Simplex Multiplier State

source_witnesses.locator: 2. The Dual Simplex Method p. 152

assumptions_latex: The primal problem is \(\max\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax=b,\ x\ge0\}\).
\(B\) is a basis and \(y_B=A_B^{-\mathsf T}c_B\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\bar c(B)=c-A^{\mathsf T}y_B\), with \(\bar c_B(B)=0\).

notation.meaning: The simplex multiplier associated with the basis.
The full vector of reduced costs.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Reduced-cost representation using the maximization sign convention.

source_refs.locator: 2. The Primal Simplex Method p. 91

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The reduced-cost state associated with \(B\) is \[\bar c(B)=c-A^{\mathsf T}y_B=c-A^{\mathsf T}A_B^{-\mathsf T}c_B.\] For every basic index \(i\in B\), the defining multiplier equations give \(\bar c_i(B)=0\). For a nonbasic index \(j\in N\), \(\bar c_j(B)=c_j-a_j^{\mathsf T}y_B\) is the objective-rate coefficient obtained when \(x_j\) increases and the basic variables change to preserve \(Ax=b\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Reduced costs subtract the multiplier-valued column prices from objective coefficients; all basic reduced costs are zero.
knowledge_statements.title: Reduced-Cost State

source_witnesses.locator: 2. The Primal Simplex Method p. 91

children.title: Primal-Feasible Basis State
children.top_down_role: Basis states satisfying the primal feasibility tests.

assumptions_latex: The constraints are \(Ax=b\) and \(x\ge0\), with \(A_B\) nonsingular.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(B\) is primal feasible if and only if \(A_B^{-1}b\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Primal feasibility predicate for a standard-form basis state.

source_refs.locator: 2. The Primal Simplex Method p. 91

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The basis state \(B\) is primal feasible when its associated basic solution, defined by \[x_B=A_B^{-1}b,\qquad x_N=0,\] satisfies the nonnegativity constraints. Equivalently, the complete primal-feasibility predicate is \(A_B^{-1}b\ge0\), interpreted componentwise. This condition involves the basic primal values only; it imposes no sign condition on the reduced costs and therefore does not by itself certify optimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A basis is primal feasible exactly when its basic solution has no negative basic component.
knowledge_statements.title: Primal-Feasible Basis State

source_witnesses.locator: 2. The Primal Simplex Method p. 91

children.title: Dual-Feasible Basis State
children.top_down_role: Basis states satisfying the dual feasibility tests.

assumptions_latex: The primal problem is \(\max\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax=b,\ x\ge0\}\).
\(B\) is a basis with multiplier \(y_B=A_B^{-\mathsf T}c_B\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(B\) is dual feasible if and only if \(A^{\mathsf T}y_B\ge c\), equivalently \(\bar c_N(B)\le0\).

notation.meaning: The multiplier determined by the basis.
Reduced costs under the maximization convention.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dual feasibility predicate under the maximization reduced-cost convention.

source_refs.locator: 4. The Dual Simplex Method p. 100

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The basis state \(B\) is dual feasible when its multiplier satisfies the dual inequalities \[A^{\mathsf T}y_B\ge c.\] Since \(A_B^{\mathsf T}y_B=c_B\), the basic inequalities hold at equality. Consequently, dual feasibility is equivalent to \(\bar c_N=c_N-A_N^{\mathsf T}y_B\le0\), interpreted componentwise. This predicate imposes no requirement that \(A_B^{-1}b\) be nonnegative.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A basis is dual feasible exactly when every nonbasic reduced cost is nonpositive under the maximization convention.
knowledge_statements.title: Dual-Feasible Basis State

source_witnesses.locator: 4. The Dual Simplex Method p. 100

children.title: Primal–Dual Feasible Basis State
children.top_down_role: Basis states simultaneously feasible from both perspectives.

knowledge_statements.title: Primal–Dual Feasible Basis State
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Simultaneous primal and dual feasibility of a standard-form basis state, with optimality as its consequence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A basis state \(B\) is primal–dual feasible precisely when \[A_B^{-1}b\ge0\qquad\text{and}\qquad \bar c_N=c_N-A_N^{\mathsf T}y_B\le0.\] Then \(x(B)\), formed from \(x_B=A_B^{-1}b\) and \(x_N=0\), is primal feasible, while \(y_B\) is dual feasible. Moreover, \(c^{\mathsf T}x(B)=c_B^{\mathsf T}A_B^{-1}b=b^{\mathsf T}y_B\), so both solutions are optimal and have zero primal–dual objective gap.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A basis state is primal–dual feasible exactly when its basic values are nonnegative and its nonbasic reduced costs are nonpositive; such a state also certifies optimality.
assumptions_latex: The primal problem is \(\max\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax=b,\ x\ge0\}\).
\(B\) is a basis with \(x_B=A_B^{-1}b\), \(y_B=A_B^{-\mathsf T}c_B\), and \(\bar c=c-A^{\mathsf T}y_B\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(B\) is primal–dual feasible if and only if \(A_B^{-1}b\ge0\) and \(\bar c_N\le0\); consequently, the associated primal and dual solutions are optimal and satisfy \(c^{\mathsf T}x(B)=b^{\mathsf T}y_B\).

notation.meaning: The basic primal solution with nonbasic entries zero.

source_refs.locator: 2. The Primal Simplex Method p. 91
4. The Dual Simplex Method p. 100

source_witnesses.locator: 2. The Primal Simplex Method p. 91
4. The Dual Simplex Method p. 100

children.title: Mixed-Feasibility Basis State
children.top_down_role: Basis states feasible from only one perspective or neither.

assumptions_latex: The primal problem is \(\max\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax=b,\ x\ge0\}\).
\(B\) is a basis with \(x_B=A_B^{-1}b\) and \(\bar c_N=c_N-A_N^{\mathsf T}A_B^{-\mathsf T}c_B\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(B\) has mixed feasibility exactly when one or both predicates fail: \(x_B\not\ge0\) or \(\bar c_N\not\le0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Complement of simultaneous primal-dual feasibility in the basis-state taxonomy.

source_refs.locator: 4. The Dual Simplex Method p. 100

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A basis state has mixed feasibility when it is not simultaneously primal and dual feasible. Under the maximization convention, this means \[A_B^{-1}b\not\ge0\quad\text{or}\quad c_N-A_N^{\mathsf T}A_B^{-\mathsf T}c_B\not\le0.\] The category therefore contains primal-feasible but dual-infeasible states, dual-feasible but primal-infeasible states, and states infeasible on both sides. Such a state alone is not an optimality certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A mixed-feasibility state violates primal feasibility, dual feasibility, or both, and therefore does not itself certify optimality.
knowledge_statements.title: Mixed-Feasibility Basis State

source_witnesses.locator: 4. The Dual Simplex Method p. 100

children.title: Basis-Derived Certificate Families
children.top_down_role: Basis-state certificate interfaces retained locally; general alternative theorems and duality proofs are external.

assumptions_latex: The primal problem is \(\max\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax=b,\ x\ge0\}\).
\(B\) is a basis satisfying \(x_B=A_B^{-1}b\ge0\) and \(\bar c_N=c_N-A_N^{\mathsf T}A_B^{-\mathsf T}c_B\le0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The pair \((x(B),y_B)\) certifies \(x(B)\) optimal because it is primal-dual feasible and \(c^{\mathsf T}x(B)=b^{\mathsf T}y_B\).

notation.meaning: The basic feasible solution induced by the basis.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Basis-derived primal-dual certificate for a standard-form maximization problem.

source_refs.locator: 2. The Primal Simplex Method p. 91

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Construct \(x(B)\) by setting \(x_B=A_B^{-1}b\) and \(x_N=0\), and construct \(y_B=A_B^{-\mathsf T}c_B\). The displayed sign conditions make \(x(B)\) primal feasible and \(y_B\) dual feasible. Their objectives agree because \[c^{\mathsf T}x(B)=c_B^{\mathsf T}A_B^{-1}b=b^{\mathsf T}A_B^{-\mathsf T}c_B=b^{\mathsf T}y_B.\] Hence \((x(B),y_B)\), verifiable through basis solves and sign tests, certifies that \(x(B)\) is primal optimal and \(y_B\) is dual optimal.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nonnegative basic values and nonpositive reduced costs yield matching feasible primal and dual solutions, forming a directly checkable optimality certificate.

children.title: Tableau Simplex Representations

children.title: Constraint-Coefficient Block
children.top_down_role: Tableau region carrying transformed constraint coefficients.

knowledge_statements.title: Constraint-Coefficient Block
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Normalized constraint block for an equality-form maximization problem at a fixed basis.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \\(\\max\\{c^\\top x:Ax=b,\\ x\\ge 0\\}\\), where \\(A\\in\\mathbb R^{m\\times n}\\), and let \\(B=A_{[:,\\mathcal B]}\\) be a nonsingular basis matrix. Partition \\(A=[B\\ N]\\) according to \\(\\mathcal B\\) and its complement \\(\\mathcal N\\). Multiplying the constraints by \\(B^{-1}\\) produces the normalized constraint-coefficient block \\[\\bar A:=B^{-1}A=[I_m\\; B^{-1}N].\\] Its column \\(\\bar a_j=B^{-1}a_j\\) gives the coordinates of the original column \\(a_j\\) in the ordered basis \\(B\\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The constraint block is obtained by premultiplying every constraint column by the inverse basis; basic columns become the identity and nonbasic columns become their basis coordinates.
assumptions_latex: \\(A\\in\\mathbb R^{m\\times n}\\) has row rank \\(m\\).
\\(B=A_{[:,\\mathcal B]}\\) is nonsingular.

notation.meaning: Ordered basic and nonbasic index sets.
Basic and nonbasic column blocks of A.

children.title: Basis-Column Block

knowledge_statements.title: Basis-Column Block
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Identity-column structure of the normalized tableau under an ordered basis.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the equality-form system \\(Ax=b\\), choose an ordered basis \\(\\mathcal B=(i_1,\\ldots,i_m)\\) with \\(B=[a_{i_1}\\ \\cdots\\ a_{i_m}]\\) nonsingular. In the basis-normalized block \\(\\bar A=B^{-1}A\\), the basic-column submatrix satisfies \\[\\bar A_{[:,\\mathcal B]}=B^{-1}B=I_m.\\] Consequently, the column belonging to basic variable \\(x_{i_k}\\) is the unit vector \\(e_k\\). This identity block records both which variables are basic and their row ordering in the canonical tableau.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: After basis normalization, the basic columns form an identity matrix; each basic variable has a unique unit column aligned with its tableau row.
assumptions_latex: \\(B=[a_{i_1}\\ \\cdots\\ a_{i_m}]\\) is nonsingular.
The tableau row order agrees with the ordered basis \\(\\mathcal B\\).

notation.meaning: Index of the basic variable assigned to row k.
The kth standard unit vector in Euclidean m-space.

children.title: Constraint-to-Basis Block Alignment
children.top_down_role: Positional correspondence between constraint rows plus basic columns.

knowledge_statements.title: Constraint-to-Basis Block Alignment
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Ordering condition coupling constraint rows, identity columns, and basic variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \\(\\mathcal B=(i_1,\\ldots,i_m)\\) be an ordered basis for \\(Ax=b\\), and let \\(B=[a_{i_1}\\ \\cdots\\ a_{i_m}]\\). A canonical constraint block is aligned with \\(\\mathcal B\\) precisely when its rows are ordered so that \\[B^{-1}a_{i_k}=e_k\\qquad(k=1,\\ldots,m),\\] and its right-hand-side entry in row \\(k\\) is \\((B^{-1}b)_k\\). Under this alignment, row \\(k\\) represents the solved equation for \\(x_{i_k}\\); simultaneously permuting basis indices and the corresponding rows preserves alignment.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Alignment means that row k solves for the kth ordered basic variable, whose normalized column is the kth unit vector and whose value is the kth normalized right-hand side.
assumptions_latex: \\(A\\in\\mathbb R^{m\\times n}\\) and \\(B\\) is nonsingular.
Basic variables and tableau rows are each given an explicit order.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Row \\(k\\) is aligned with \\(x_{i_k}\\) exactly when \\(B^{-1}a_{i_k}=e_k\\) and its constant is \\((B^{-1}b)_k\\).

children.title: Objective-Value Block
children.top_down_role: Tableau region carrying the current objective-state value.

knowledge_statements.title: Objective-Value Block
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Constant objective entry associated with a fixed primal basis.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \\(\\max\\{c^\\top x:Ax=b,\\ x\\ge0\\}\\), partition \\(x=(x_B,x_N)\\) and \\(c=(c_B,c_N)\\) using a nonsingular basis \\(B\\). Substitution of \\(x_B=B^{-1}b-B^{-1}Nx_N\\) into the objective gives \\[c^\\top x=\\bar z+r_N^\\top x_N,\\qquad \\bar z:=c_B^\\top B^{-1}b.\\] The scalar \\(\\bar z\\) is the objective-value block. At the associated basic solution \\(x_N=0\\), it equals the objective value \\(c^\\top x=\\bar z\\), irrespective of whether that basic solution is feasible.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The objective-value block is the basic-cost row applied to the normalized right-hand side; it equals the objective at the associated basic solution.
assumptions_latex: \\(B\\) is a nonsingular basis submatrix of \\(A\\).
Variables and costs are partitioned conformably into basic and nonbasic parts.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \\(\\bar z=c_B^\\top B^{-1}b\\), and \\(c^\\top x=\\bar z\\) when \\(x_N=0\\).

notation.meaning: Cost vector of the basic variables.
Objective constant associated with the basis.

children.title: Reduced-Cost Block

knowledge_statements.title: Reduced-Cost Block
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Reduced objective coefficients for a maximization problem in canonical basis coordinates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \\(\\max\\{c^\\top x:Ax=b,\\ x\\ge0\\}\\) with nonsingular basis \\(B\\), define the simplex multiplier by \\(y^\\top=c_B^\\top B^{-1}\\). The full reduced-cost block and its nonbasic part are \\[r^\\top:=c^\\top-y^\\top A,\\qquad r_N^\\top=c_N^\\top-c_B^\\top B^{-1}N.\\] Basic reduced costs vanish because \\(r_B^\\top=c_B^\\top-c_B^\\top B^{-1}B=0\\). Hence the canonical objective row is \\(c^\\top x=\\bar z+r_N^\\top x_N\\), where \\(\\bar z=c_B^\\top B^{-1}b\\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Reduced costs are original costs minus prices induced by the current basis; basic reduced costs are zero, while nonbasic reduced costs govern objective change.
assumptions_latex: \\(B\\) is a nonsingular basis submatrix of \\(A\\).
The problem uses the maximization and reduced-cost sign convention displayed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \\(r^\\top=c^\\top-c_B^\\top B^{-1}A\\), with \\(r_B=0\\) and \\(r_N^\\top=c_N^\\top-c_B^\\top B^{-1}N\\).

notation.meaning: Simplex multiplier associated with the basis.

knowledge_statements.title: Reduced-Cost Sign Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Optimality and improvement signs for equality-form maximization with nonnegative variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \\(x_B=B^{-1}b\\ge0\\) be a primal-feasible basic solution of \\(\\max\\{c^\\top x:Ax=b,\\ x\\ge0\\}\\), and use \\(r_N^\\top=c_N^\\top-c_B^\\top B^{-1}N\\). If \\(r_N\\le0\\) componentwise, the basis is optimal. If some \\(r_j>0\\), increasing nonbasic \\(x_j\\) locally improves the objective; a finite primal pivot requires at least one positive component of \\(B^{-1}a_j\\). If \\(r_j>0\\) and \\(B^{-1}a_j\\le0\\), then the feasible ray obtained by increasing \\(x_j\\) proves that the maximization problem is unbounded above.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a feasible maximization basis, nonpositive reduced costs certify optimality; a positive reduced cost permits improvement and may certify unboundedness when its normalized column is nonpositive.
assumptions_latex: Reduced costs use \\(r_j=c_j-c_B^\\top B^{-1}a_j\\).
All primal variables are constrained nonnegative.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \\(r_N\\le0\\) certifies optimality; \\(r_j>0\\) with \\(B^{-1}a_j\\le0\\) certifies unboundedness above.

notation.meaning: Reduced cost of nonbasic variable j.

knowledge_statements.title: Right-Hand-Side State
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Basis-normalized constants and the primal-feasibility state they encode.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \\(Ax=b\\) and a nonsingular basis \\(B\\), the canonical tableau right-hand-side state is \\[\\bar b:=B^{-1}b.\\] With nonbasic variables fixed at zero, the associated basic solution is \\(x_B=\\bar b\\) and \\(x_N=0\\). Under the nonnegativity restrictions \\(x\\ge0\\), this basic solution is primal feasible if and only if \\(\\bar b\\ge0\\) componentwise. More generally, the normalized constraint equations are \\(x_B=\\bar b-B^{-1}Nx_N\\), so \\(\\bar b\\) is the constant column of both the canonical tableau and its dictionary.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The right-hand-side state is the basis-normalized vector of constants; it gives current basic-variable values and determines primal feasibility by componentwise nonnegativity.
assumptions_latex: \\(B\\) is a nonsingular basis submatrix of \\(A\\).
The primal variables satisfy \\(x\\ge0\\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \\(\\bar b=B^{-1}b\\), and the associated basic solution is feasible exactly when \\(\\bar b\\ge0\\).

knowledge_statements.title: Canonical Dictionary Representation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Solved-equation form of a simplex basis state for an equality-form maximization problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \\(\\max\\{c^\\top x:Ax=b,\\ x\\ge0\\}\\), partition \\(A=[B\\ N]\\), \\(x=(x_B,x_N)\\), and \\(c=(c_B,c_N)\\), with \\(B\\) nonsingular. The canonical dictionary associated with \\(B\\) is \\[x_B=\\bar b-\\bar N x_N,\\qquad z=\\bar z+r_N^\\top x_N,\\] where \\(\\bar b=B^{-1}b\\), \\(\\bar N=B^{-1}N\\), \\(\\bar z=c_B^\\top B^{-1}b\\), and \\(r_N^\\top=c_N^\\top-c_B^\\top B^{-1}N\\). Setting \\(x_N=0\\) recovers the basis state \\(x_B=\\bar b\\) and objective value \\(z=\\bar z\\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A canonical dictionary solves the constraints for basic variables and expresses the objective as its current value plus reduced-cost-weighted nonbasic variables.
assumptions_latex: \\(B\\) is a nonsingular \\(m\\times m\\) column submatrix of \\(A\\).
Variables and objective coefficients are partitioned conformably.

notation.meaning: Current basic values and objective constant.

knowledge_statements.title: Matrix Tableau Representation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Augmented matrix encoding of the canonical dictionary under a fixed sign convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given the canonical dictionary \\(x_B=\\bar b-\\bar N x_N\\) and \\(z=\\bar z+r_N^\\top x_N\\), its matrix tableau, with columns ordered as \\((x_B,x_N,z,\\mathrm{rhs})\\), is \\[T_B=\\left[\\begin{array}{ccc|c}I_m&\\bar N&0&\\bar b\\\\0&-r_N^\\top&1&\\bar z\\end{array}\\right].\\] Each constraint row represents \\(x_B+\\bar N x_N=\\bar b\\), and the last row represents \\(z-r_N^\\top x_N=\\bar z\\). Thus reading the rows as equations recovers the dictionary uniquely, while writing those equations coefficientwise recovers \\(T_B\\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The matrix tableau stores the dictionary’s constraint and objective equations as rows; under fixed column and sign conventions, either representation uniquely determines the other.
assumptions_latex: A canonical dictionary with blocks \\(\\bar N,\\bar b,r_N,\\bar z\\) is given.
Columns are ordered as \\((x_B,x_N,z,\\mathrm{rhs})\\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \\(T_B\\) and the equations \\(x_B=\\bar b-\\bar N x_N\\), \\(z=\\bar z+r_N^\\top x_N\\) are equivalent representations.

notation.meaning: Canonical matrix tableau for basis B.

knowledge_statements.title: Primal Tableau Pivots
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Single-column primal-simplex pivot preserving feasibility for a maximization tableau.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Start from a primal-feasible dictionary \\(x_B=\\bar b-\\bar N x_N\\), \\(\\bar b\\ge0\\). Choose an entering index \\(j\\in\\mathcal N\\) with \\(r_j>0\\). If \\(\\bar N_{ij}\\le0\\) for every row \\(i\\), report unboundedness. Otherwise choose a leaving row \\[p\\in\\operatorname*{argmin}_{i:\\bar N_{ij}>0}\\frac{\\bar b_i}{\\bar N_{ij}}.\\] Pivot on the nonzero coefficient \\(\\bar N_{pj}\\): solve row \\(p\\) for \\(x_j\\), substitute it into every other constraint row and the objective row, and exchange \\(j\\) with the basic index of row \\(p\\). The resulting dictionary remains primal feasible.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A primal pivot enters a positive-reduced-cost variable, uses the minimum-ratio test to choose the leaving row, and algebraically exchanges the two variables while preserving feasibility.
assumptions_latex: The current dictionary satisfies \\(\\bar b\\ge0\\).
The problem is a maximization problem with reduced-cost convention \\(z=\\bar z+r_N^\\top x_N\\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The pivoted dictionary represents the adjacent basis and has a nonnegative right-hand-side state.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: One Full-Tableau Primal Simplex Iteration
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Primal simplex pivot performed using an explicit tableau, including optimality and unboundedness tests.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the tableau associated with a basis matrix \(B\) and its basic feasible solution \(x\), inspect the reduced costs in row zero. If all are nonnegative, terminate with \(x\) optimal. Otherwise choose \(j\) with \(\bar c_j<0\) and let \(u=B^{-1}A_j\), the pivot column. If \(u_i\le0\) for every \(i\), terminate with optimal value \(-\infty\). Otherwise choose \(\ell\in\arg\min_{i:u_i>0}x_{B(i)}/u_i\), let \(A_j\) enter and \(A_{B(\ell)}\) leave the basis, and apply row operations using pivot row \(\ell\) so that the pivot element becomes one and every other entry in the pivot column becomes zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In a full simplex tableau, nonnegative reduced costs certify that the current basic feasible solution is optimal. Otherwise, select a column with negative reduced cost. If its tableau column has no positive entry, the LP is unbounded below. If it has a positive entry, apply the minimum-ratio test to choose the leaving row, exchange the entering and leaving columns, and perform a Gauss–Jordan pivot that turns the pivot column into the corresponding unit vector.
assumptions_latex: \min\{c^\top x:Ax=b,\ x\ge0\}\text{ is in primal standard form.}
B\text{ is a nonsingular basis matrix.}
x\text{ is the basic feasible solution associated with }B.
\text{The full tableau for }B\text{ is available.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \bar c\ge0\Rightarrow x\text{ is optimal};\qquad \bar c_j<0\ \land\ B^{-1}A_j\le0\Rightarrow \inf c^\top x=-\infty;\qquad\text{otherwise a minimum-ratio Gauss--Jordan pivot yields the next primal tableau basis.

knowledge_statements.title: Dual Tableau Pivots
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Single-row dual-simplex pivot preserving reduced-cost optimality for a maximization tableau.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Start from \\(x_B=\\bar b-\\bar N x_N\\), \\(z=\\bar z+r_N^\\top x_N\\), with \\(r_N\\le0\\) but some \\(\\bar b_p<0\\). Choose such a leaving row \\(p\\). Eligible entering indices satisfy \\(\\bar N_{pj}<0\\); if none exists, report primal infeasibility. Choose \\[j\\in\\operatorname*{argmin}_{k:\\bar N_{pk}<0}\\frac{r_k}{\\bar N_{pk}}.\\] Pivot on \\(\\bar N_{pj}\\), solving row \\(p\\) for \\(x_j\\), substituting into all other rows, and exchanging \\(j\\) with the basic index of row \\(p\\). The new reduced costs remain nonpositive; repeated pivots seek \\(\\bar b\\ge0\\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A dual pivot repairs a negative basic value while preserving nonpositive reduced costs, using a ratio test over negative coefficients in the leaving row.
assumptions_latex: The reduced-cost state satisfies \\(r_N\\le0\\).
At least one basic value is negative.
The maximization dictionary uses the displayed sign convention.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: An eligible ratio-test pivot preserves \\(r_N\\le0\\); absence of an eligible entering column certifies primal infeasibility.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: One Tableau Iteration of the Dual Simplex Method
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Stopping tests, pivot selection, and tableau update from a dual-feasible basis state with nonnegative reduced costs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Start with a tableau associated with a basis matrix \(B\) and reduced costs \(\bar c_i\ge 0\). If \(B^{-1}b\ge 0\), terminate with an optimal basic feasible solution. Otherwise choose \(\ell\) such that \(x_{B(\ell)}<0\), and denote the pivot-row entries by \(v_i\). If \(v_i\ge 0\) for every \(i\), terminate with optimal dual cost \(+\infty\). Otherwise choose any \(j\in\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{i:v_i<0}\bar c_i/|v_i|\), replace \(A_{B(\ell)}\) by \(A_j\) in the basis, and perform tableau row operations that make the pivot entry one and all other entries in its column zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: From a basis tableau with nonnegative reduced costs, terminate optimally if every basic value is nonnegative. Otherwise select a row with a negative basic value. If that row has no negative coefficient, terminate because the optimal dual cost is positive infinity. Otherwise enter a column attaining the minimum reduced-cost ratio, remove the selected basic column, and pivot to restore canonical tableau form.
assumptions_latex: B\text{ is the current basis matrix.}
\bar c_i\ge 0\quad\text{for every tableau column }i.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: B^{-1}b\ge 0\Rightarrow\text{optimal termination};\quad x_{B(\ell)}<0\land(\forall i,\,v_i\ge 0)\Rightarrow z_D^*=+\infty;\quad\text{otherwise }j\in\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{i:v_i<0}\frac{\bar c_i}{|v_i|}\text{ defines the pivot.}

knowledge_statements.title: Block Tableau Pivots
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Simultaneous exchange of equally sized basic and nonbasic index blocks.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In a dictionary \\(x_B=\\bar b-\\bar N x_N\\), choose basic positions \\(P\\subseteq\\{1,\\ldots,m\\}\\) and nonbasic indices \\(Q\\subseteq\\mathcal N\\) with \\(|P|=|Q|\\) and pivot block \\(H:=\\bar N_{P,Q}\\) nonsingular. Partition the selected equations as \\[x_{B_P}=\\bar b_P-Hx_Q-\\bar N_{P,\\mathcal N\\setminus Q}x_{\\mathcal N\\setminus Q}.\\] Solve this block system for \\(x_Q\\) using \\(H^{-1}\\), substitute the result into the remaining constraint equations and the objective equation, and exchange \\(x_{B_P}\\) with \\(x_Q\\). The output is an algebraically equivalent dictionary for the block-updated basis.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A block pivot simultaneously exchanges equally many basic and nonbasic variables by solving a nonsingular pivot subsystem and substituting it throughout the dictionary.
assumptions_latex: \\(P\\) and \\(Q\\) have equal cardinality.
The pivot block \\(H=\\bar N_{P,Q}\\) is nonsingular.
The exchanged columns form a valid updated basis.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Block elimination using \\(H^{-1}\\) yields an equivalent canonical dictionary with basic set \\((\\mathcal B\\setminus B_P)\\cup Q\\).

knowledge_statements.title: Implicit Tableau Columns
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Recovery of simplex tableau columns from basis solves without materializing the full tableau.

Consider the standard-form problem

knowledge_statements.title: Implicit Objective Row
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Recovery of the simplex objective row through a transposed basis solve.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\min\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax=b,\ x\ge0\}\) with nonsingular basis \(B\), define the simplex multiplier \(y\) by the transposed solve \(B^{\mathsf T}y=c_{\mathcal B}\). The implicit objective-row coefficient of column \(a_j\) is the reduced cost \(\bar c_j=c_j-a_j^{\mathsf T}y\). Consequently, for nonbasic variables \(x_{\mathcal N}\), the objective identity is \(c^{\mathsf T}x=c_{\mathcal B}^{\mathsf T}B^{-1}b+\bar c_{\mathcal N}^{\mathsf T}x_{\mathcal N}\), while \(\bar c_j=0\) for every basic index \(j\in\mathcal B\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Solve the transposed basis system for the simplex multipliers, then obtain any objective-row entry by subtracting the column’s multiplier product from its cost.
assumptions_latex: \(B=A_{[:,\mathcal B]}\) is nonsingular.

knowledge_statements.title: Selective Tableau Extraction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extraction of requested tableau entries using basis-factorization solves.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), \(b\in\mathbb R^m\), \(c\in\mathbb R^n\), a basic index set \(\mathcal B\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}\) of cardinality \(m\), the nonsingular basis \(B=A_{[:,\mathcal B]}\) with a solve-capable factorization, requested rows \(I\subseteq\{1,\ldots,m\}\), and requested columns \(J\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}\). For each \(j\in J\), solve \(Bt_j=A_{[:,j]}\) and retain only \((t_j)_I\). If requested, solve \(Br=b\) and retain \(r_I\). If objective-row entries are requested, solve \(B^{\mathsf T}y=c_{\mathcal B}\) once and return \(\bar c_j=c_j-A_{[:,j]}^{\mathsf T}y\) for each requested \(j\). Stop after returning the requested entries; no unrequested tableau column is formed.

knowledge_statements.title: Small Dense Tableau Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Resource condition under which an explicit dense tableau is computationally admissible.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(m\) constraints and \(n\) variables, let \(E=(m+1)(n+1)\) be the number of scalar positions in the chosen full-tableau convention. Let \(M\) be the available scalar-word storage, let \(C\) be the permitted arithmetic operations per pivot, and let \(K>0\) be a fixed constant such that the dense Gauss–Jordan pivot implementation uses at most \(KE\) operations. The small dense tableau regime is the condition \(E\le M\) and \(KE\le C\). Under this unit-cost model, the tableau fits in storage and a dense pivot fits the stated per-pivot budget; its asymptotic storage and pivot work are both \(\Theta(mn)\).

The selected pivot implementation uses at most \(K(m+1)(n+1)\) operations for a fixed \(K>0\).

knowledge_statements.title: Educational Tableau Use
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explicit tableau representation for tracing simplex algebra and pivot effects.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(\min\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax=b,\ x\ge0\}\), where \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), \(b\in\mathbb R^m\), and \(c\in\mathbb R^n\). Let \(\mathcal B\) be a basic index set, let \(\mathcal N\) be its complement, and write \(A=[B\ A_{\mathcal N}]\) after ordering the basic columns first, with \(B=A_{[:,\mathcal B]}\) nonsingular. The explicit dictionary is \(x_{\mathcal B}=B^{-1}b-B^{-1}A_{\mathcal N}x_{\mathcal N}\) and \(c^{\mathsf T}x=c_{\mathcal B}^{\mathsf T}B^{-1}b+\bar c_{\mathcal N}^{\mathsf T}x_{\mathcal N}\), where \(\bar c_{\mathcal N}=c_{\mathcal N}-A_{\mathcal N}^{\mathsf T}B^{-\mathsf T}c_{\mathcal B}\). A simplex pivot on an eligible nonzero tableau entry is a Gauss–Jordan elimination step exchanging one basic and one nonbasic variable while preserving these equations. Displaying the coefficients permits direct tracing of the basic solution, reduced costs, ratio-test data, and updated basis dictionary.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a specified standard-form linear program and basis, the full dictionary displays the quantities used in a simplex pivot and allows the basis exchange and its algebraic effects to be traced directly.

knowledge_statements.title: Audit Tableau Use

It does not by itself certify primal feasibility, dual feasibility, or optimality unless their corresponding sign conditions are checked separately.

knowledge_statements.title: Tableau Transparency Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Limit of transparency gained by explicitly displaying all transformed simplex coefficients.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An explicit tableau makes the current transformed equations transparent only while its \((m+1)(n+1)\) entries can be materialized and inspected within the available resources. Moreover, the displayed matrix \(B^{-1}A\) need not preserve the sparsity of \(A\) or expose the factorization and numerical conditioning of \(B\). Hence tableau visibility certifies algebraic relationships among displayed coefficients, but it does not by itself reveal sparse computational cost, numerical stability, or provenance of rounding errors. Beyond the storage and inspection budget, selective basis solves define the same quantities without full visual transparency.

Computational transparency means direct inspection of stored transformed coefficients.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Explicit visibility of \(B^{-1}A\) is bounded by \(\Theta(mn)\) materialization and does not imply visibility of sparse or numerical structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Full-Tableau Storage Burden
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dense storage requirement for an explicitly materialized simplex tableau.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(m\) equality constraints and \(n\) variables, a conventional full tableau containing the transformed constraint coefficients, right-hand side, objective coefficients, and objective value has \((m+1)(n+1)\) scalar positions, up to convention-dependent omitted or auxiliary fields. Dense explicit storage therefore requires \(\Theta(mn)\) scalar words. This bound counts materialized tableau entries and excludes separate storage for the original problem data, basis indices, and numerical workspace. Any representation retaining every tableau coefficient explicitly has an information-storage lower bound of \(\Omega(mn)\) scalar positions in the generic dense case.

children.title: Tableau Fill Growth
children.top_down_role: Loss of sparsity during explicit tableau transformations.

knowledge_statements.title: Tableau Fill Growth
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sparse original matrices can yield substantially denser transformed tableau matrices.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S\in\mathbb R^{m\times m}\) have ones on its first subdiagonal and zeros elsewhere, and set \(B=I-S\). Then \(B\) has \(2m-1\) nonzeros, whereas \(B^{-1}=I+S+\cdots+S^{m-1}\) has \(m(m+1)/2\) nonzeros. If \(A=[B\ I]\), then \(A\) has only \(3m-1\) nonzeros, but the transformed tableau is \(B^{-1}A=[I\ B^{-1}]\), containing \(\Theta(m^2)\) nonzeros. Thus forming a tableau can produce quadratic fill even from a linearly sparse constraint matrix.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A sparse basis can have a dense inverse, so transforming a sparse constraint matrix into tableau form can create quadratic fill.
assumptions_latex: Tableau fill counts nonzero scalar entries.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There exist matrices with \(\operatorname{nnz}(A)=\Theta(m)\) but \(\operatorname{nnz}(B^{-1}A)=\Theta(m^2)\).

notation.meaning: Number of nonzero entries of a matrix.

knowledge_statements.title: Explicit-Tableau Scale Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Resource boundary separating explicit tableaux from basis-factorization implementations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under dense storage and arithmetic, an explicit tableau for \(m\) constraints and \(n\) variables requires \(\Theta(mn)\) words and a Gauss–Jordan pivot requires \(\Theta(mn)\) arithmetic operations. Therefore, if either available storage is \(o(mn)\) or the permitted work per simplex iteration is \(o(mn)\), a full explicit tableau cannot satisfy the corresponding resource bound. This boundary concerns the representation, not the simplex method itself: a revised implementation may retain a basis factorization and recover columns or reduced costs selectively without materializing all \(mn\) transformed coefficients.

A pivot updates a constant fraction of tableau entries.

knowledge_statements.title: Basis-Solve Primal State
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Revised-simplex representation of the current primal basic solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the standard-form constraints \(Ax=b\), \(x\ge0\), let \(\mathcal B\) index \(m\) linearly independent columns and let \(B=A_{[:,\mathcal B]}\). The revised-simplex primal state is obtained by solving \(Bx_{\mathcal B}=b\) and setting \(x_{\mathcal N}=0\). This vector satisfies \(Ax=b\) because \(Ax=Bx_{\mathcal B}\). It is a primal basic feasible solution exactly when \(x_{\mathcal B}\ge0\). The state can be maintained using a factorization of \(B\), without storing \(B^{-1}\) or a full tableau.

knowledge_statements.title: Transposed-Basis-Solve Dual State
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Revised-simplex representation of multipliers and reduced costs through a transposed solve.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\min\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax=b,\ x\ge0\}\) and nonsingular basis \(B=A_{[:,\mathcal B]}\), the revised-simplex dual state is the unique vector \(y\) satisfying \(B^{\mathsf T}y=c_{\mathcal B}\). Its associated reduced costs are \(\bar c=c-A^{\mathsf T}y\), with \(\bar c_{\mathcal B}=0\). Under this minimization convention, \(y\) is dual feasible exactly when \(A^{\mathsf T}y\le c\), equivalently \(\bar c\ge0\). Both \(y\) and selected reduced costs can be computed from a factorization of \(B\) without forming \(B^{-1}\).

Otherwise choose a leaving position \(r\) with \((x_{\mathcal B})_r<0\), solve \(B^{\mathsf T}w=e_r\), and compute \(\alpha_j=w^{\mathsf T}a_j\) for each \(j\in\mathcal N\). If no nonbasic \(j\) satisfies \(\alpha_j<0\), then \(w^{\mathsf T}A\geq 0\) and \(w^{\mathsf T}b<0\), which certify primal infeasibility. Otherwise choose \(j\in\arg\max_{k\in\mathcal N:\alpha_k<0}\bar c_k/\alpha_k\), resolving ties by the stipulated anti-cycling rule, pivot \(j\) into the basis, update the factorization and reduced costs, and repeat.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Partition \(\mathcal N\) into groups \(G_1,\ldots,G_q\) and initialize a group pointer \(k\). Price only indices in \(G_k\). If an index with \(\bar c_j<0\) is found, select an entering variable according to the local pricing rule and perform the simplex pivot; subsequent pricing resumes from a prescribed current or successor group. If no improving index is found, advance cyclically to the next group. Stop as optimal only after every group has been scanned without finding a negative reduced cost for the unchanged basis and pricing state.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Partial pricing scans rotating subsets of nonbasic columns and declares optimality only after every subset has been checked for the unchanged basis without finding improvement.
knowledge_statements.title: Partial Pricing

source_witnesses.locator: 7. Partial Pricing p. 143

assumptions_latex: The current basis is primal feasible.
A pricing pass can identify several nonbasic variables with improving reduced costs.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Global optimality is asserted only after refreshed pricing finds no improving nonbasic variable.

notation.meaning: Selected working set of improving indices
Maximum number of locally processed candidates

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic working-set form of multiple pricing.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Perform a pricing pass and choose a working set \(W\) containing at most \(p\) improving nonbasic indices. Select an entering variable from \(W\), compute its current basis direction, apply the ratio test, and pivot. After the pivot, update or recompute the reduced costs of the remaining candidates and remove every index that is basic, no longer improving, or otherwise inadmissible. Continue selecting from \(W\) until it is empty or a prescribed refresh condition holds, then perform a new global pricing pass. Terminate only when refreshed global pricing finds no improving nonbasic variable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Multiple pricing retains several improving candidates from one pricing pass, processes valid candidates locally, and periodically refreshes global reduced costs.
knowledge_statements.title: Multiple Pricing

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The working-set description is a plausible multiple-pricing family, but refresh conditions and candidate-update rules vary across implementations. A source identifying and defining this particular variant is required.

assumptions_latex: The current basis is primal feasible.
At least one nonbasic index has \(\bar c_j<0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The selected entering variable maximizes objective decrease per unit Euclidean displacement along its adjacent feasible edge.

notation.meaning: Basis direction associated with nonbasic column j

source_refs.locator: 8. Steepest Edge p. 144

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each eligible nonbasic index \(j\) with \(\bar c_j<0\), solve \(Bd_j=a_j\) and compute the edge weight \(\gamma_j=1+\lVert d_j\rVert_2^2\). Select \[j\in\arg\max_{k:\bar c_k<0}\frac{-\bar c_k}{\sqrt{\gamma_k}}.\] The associated full-space edge direction has basic part \(-d_j\), entering component \(1\), and Euclidean norm \(\sqrt{\gamma_j}\). Apply the ordinary primal ratio test to this direction, pivot, and update the basis and edge weights.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Steepest-edge pricing chooses the improving column with the greatest objective decrease per unit Euclidean edge length.

Each eligible nonbasic index has a positive surrogate edge weight.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Devex selects an improving variable by a steepest-edge score using inexpensive surrogate weights rather than exact edge norms.
