knowledge_statements.scope_note: Primal Devex as an approximate steepest-edge pricing family.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Devex pricing maintains positive weights \(w_j\) intended to approximate the exact squared edge lengths \(1+\lVert B^{-1}a_j\rVert_2^2\). Among indices satisfying \(\bar c_j<0\), it selects an entering index from \[\arg\max_j frac{-ba c_j}{sqrt{w_j}}.\] After a pivot, the weights are updated by a Devex reference-framework recurrence and are periodically reinitialized when their approximation quality deteriorates. Thus the selection criterion has the form of exact steepest-edge pricing, while avoiding a separate exact basis solve for every candidate edge weight.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Devex approximates steepest-edge pricing with positive, cheaply updated surrogate edge weights and periodically resets its reference framework.
knowledge_statements.title: Devex Pricing

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Devex belongs here as a pricing algorithm, not merely a generic principle. The record also invokes an unspecified reference-framework recurrence and reinitialization test, so an authoritative source for the intended Devex variant is needed before a precise algorithm record can be produced.

assumptions_latex: A pricing vector \(z\in\mathbb{R}^q\) must be formed or scanned.
An implementation fixes a density threshold \(\tau_d\in(0,1]\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The pricing operation is assigned to the dense regime when \(\operatorname{nnz}(z)/q\geq\tau_d\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Parametric implementation condition, not a universal numerical cutoff.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(z\in\mathbb{R}^q\) denote the vector produced or inspected by a pricing operation, such as reduced costs or a transposed-basis-solve result. For a fixed implementation threshold \(\tau_d\in(0,1]\), the operation is in the dense pricing regime when \[\operatorname{dens}(z):=frac{operatorname{nnz}(z)}{q}citau_d.\] In this regime, dense vector traversal and dense arithmetic kernels are used because work proportional to \(q\) is not avoided by sparse indexing. The value of \(\tau_d\) is a machine- and implementation-dependent policy parameter.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Pricing is dense when the relevant vector's nonzero fraction exceeds an implementation threshold, making full traversal and dense kernels appropriate.
knowledge_statements.title: Dense Pricing Regime

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: A condition is a reasonable content kind for this regime leaf, but the proposed density threshold and the asserted kernel choice are implementation policies rather than standard mathematical facts. They require an architecture or implementation source with a specific locator.

children.title: Sparse Pricing Regime
children.top_down_role: Pricing workloads with a limited active coefficient footprint.

assumptions_latex: A pricing vector \(z\in\mathbb{R}^q\) must be formed or scanned.
An implementation fixes thresholds \(0<\tau_h<\tau_d\leq1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The pricing operation is assigned to the sparse regime when \(\tau_h<\operatorname{nnz}(z)/q<\tau_d\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Intermediate sparsity regime defined relative to implementation thresholds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(z\in\mathbb{R}^q\) be the vector produced or inspected during pricing and define \(\delta(z)=\operatorname{nnz}(z)/q\). Given implementation thresholds \(0<\tau_h<\tau_d\leq1\), the sparse pricing regime is the condition \[\tau_h<delta(z)<tau_d.\] Sparse indexed storage and sparse arithmetic are then used to avoid operations on structural zeros, while the support is not small enough to invoke a hypersparse traversal strategy. Both thresholds depend on data structures, matrix structure, and hardware; they are not intrinsic constants of the linear program.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Pricing is sparse when vector density lies between implementation-specific hypersparse and dense thresholds, so indexed sparse kernels reduce work on zeros.
knowledge_statements.title: Sparse Pricing Regime

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The intermediate-regime condition fits the leaf in broad intent, but the two-threshold classification is implementation-specific and unsupported. The statement also contains undefined TeX commands. A source defining the intended sparse and hypersparse transition policy is required before mathematical and notational revision is reliable.

children.title: Hypersparse Pricing Regime
children.top_down_role: Pricing workloads with exceptionally small active supports.

knowledge_statements.title: Hypersparse Pricing Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Operational regime for revised-simplex pricing with an exceptionally small active candidate set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a bounded-variable linear program with nonbasic index set \(N\), reduced costs \(\bar c_N=c_N-A_N^{\mathsf T}B^{-\mathsf T}c_B\), and eligibility predicate \(E(j)\) determined by the optimization sense and the active bound of \(x_j\), define \(P=\{j\in N:E(j)\}\). Given a declared threshold \(0<\tau_h<1\), pricing is in the hypersparse regime when \(|P|/|N|\leq \tau_h\) and reduced-cost evaluation can be restricted to \(P\) without changing the entering variable selected by the stated pricing rule. The threshold and the mechanism maintaining \(P\) are implementation parameters, not universal mathematical constants.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Pricing is hypersparse when only a declared tiny fraction of nonbasic variables is eligible and restricting evaluation to that maintained set preserves the pricing choice.
assumptions_latex: \(B\) is a nonsingular basis matrix.
The maintained set \(P\) contains every index eligible under the stated pricing rule.
\(0<\tau_h<1\) is fixed before classification.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P\) defines the hypersparse pricing regime exactly when \(|P|/|N|\leq\tau_h\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No citation supports identifying hypersparsity with the density of pricing-eligible indices or the threshold tau_h. Hypersparsity may instead concern sparsity of computational vectors or results. The conclusion also omits the stated requirement that restricting evaluation to P preserve the pricing choice, so the authoritative definition must be established before correction.

children.title: Pricing-Sparsity Transition
children.top_down_role: Execution boundary between ordinary sparse pricing plus hypersparse pricing.

knowledge_statements.title: Pricing-Sparsity Transition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: State transition between sparse and hypersparse revised-simplex pricing implementations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(N_k\) be the nonbasic indices and \(P_k\subseteq N_k\) the maintained pricing-eligible indices at iteration \(k\). Fix thresholds \(0<\tau_{\mathrm{in}}<\tau_{\mathrm{out}}<1\) to provide hysteresis. Enter hypersparse pricing when \(|P_k|/|N_k|\leq\tau_{\mathrm{in}}\); remain there while \(|P_k|/|N_k|<\tau_{\mathrm{out}}\); and return to sparse pricing when \(|P_k|/|N_k|\geq\tau_{\mathrm{out}}\). A transition is valid only after refreshing \(P_k\) so that no pricing-eligible index is omitted. This condition classifies computational states and does not alter the mathematical pricing criterion.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Hysteretic density thresholds switch between sparse and hypersparse pricing, provided the eligible set is refreshed before each switch.
assumptions_latex: \(P_k\) contains all indices eligible for entry at iteration \(k\).
\(0<\tau_{\mathrm{in}}<\tau_{\mathrm{out}}<1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed hysteretic predicates determine the pricing-sparsity transition without changing pricing eligibility.

notation.meaning: Nonbasic index set at iteration k.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The hysteretic transition is a plausible implementation policy, but no source establishes these predicates or thresholds as the intended pricing-sparsity transition. Its mathematical version is inseparable from the unsupported definition of the hypersparse regime.

knowledge_statements.title: Primal Ratio-Test Family
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bounded-variable primal-simplex ratio test along a feasible entering direction, including the entering variable's opposite bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a primal-feasible basic solution \(x_B\), basic bounds \(l_B\leq x_B\leq u_B\), a nonbasic entering variable \(x_q\) at a bound, and \(d=B^{-1}a_q\), choose \(\sigma\in\{-1,1\}\) so that \(x_q(\theta)=x_q+\sigma\theta\) is feasible for small \(\theta\geq0\). Then \(x_B(\theta)=x_B-\sigma\theta d\). For each basic position \(i\), define \(\theta_i=(x_{B_i}-l_{B_i})/(\sigma d_i)\) when \(\sigma d_i>0\), \(\theta_i=(u_{B_i}-x_{B_i})/(-\sigma d_i)\) when \(\sigma d_i<0\), and \(\theta_i=+\infty\) otherwise. Let \(\theta_q=u_q-x_q\) when \(\sigma=1\) and \(\theta_q=x_q-l_q\) when \(\sigma=-1\), allowing \(+\infty\) for a missing opposite bound, and set \(\theta^*=\min\{\theta_q,\min_i\theta_i\}\). A finite minimizing basic index may leave; if only \(\theta_q\) attains the minimum, the move reaches the opposite bound without a basis exchange. If \(\theta_q=+\infty\), every \(\theta_i=+\infty\), and the entering direction improves the objective, the direction is an unbounded improving ray.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The bounded-variable primal ratio test takes the largest feasible step permitted by both the basic-variable bounds and the entering variable's opposite bound. A basic blocker may leave, the entering variable may flip bounds, or an improving direction with no finite blocker may establish unboundedness.
assumptions_latex: \(B\) is nonsingular and \(x_B\) satisfies its bounds.
The entering variable \(x_q\) is at a bound and the orientation \(\sigma\) is feasible for a positive initial step.
The unboundedness conclusion additionally requires that the direction improve the objective.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_B(\theta)\) and \(x_q(\theta)\) remain feasible for \(0\leq\theta\leq\theta^*\); the type of finite minimizer determines whether a basic variable blocks or the entering variable reaches its opposite bound.

notation.meaning: Entering column expressed in basis coordinates.
Step from the entering variable's current bound to its opposite bound.
Maximum primal-feasible step considering all basic and entering-variable bounds.

knowledge_statements.title: Dual Ratio-Test Family
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dual-simplex ratio test for restoring one violated basic bound while preserving dual feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider minimization with nonbasic variables at bounds and dual-feasible reduced costs in their feasible signs. Let row \(p\) be primal infeasible and let \(w^{\mathsf T}=e_p^{\mathsf T}B^{-1}A_N\). Orient the row by \(s=1\) when \(x_{B_p}<l_{B_p}\) and \(s=-1\) when \(x_{B_p}>u_{B_p}\). Form the eligible set \(J=\{j\in N:s_j\bar c_j\geq0,\;s\,s_jw_j<0\}\), where \(s_j=1\) at a lower bound and \(s_j=-1\) at an upper bound. Select \(q\in\arg\min_{j\in J}(s_j\bar c_j)/(-s\,s_jw_j)\). If \(J=\varnothing\), the chosen infeasible row yields a dual certificate of primal infeasibility under exact arithmetic.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The dual ratio test chooses an entering variable whose pivot repairs a violated basic bound while retaining the required reduced-cost signs.
assumptions_latex: The current basis is nonsingular and the nonbasic reduced costs are dual feasible.
Exactly one oriented leaving row \(p\) is selected for the test.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A minimizing \(q\) preserves dual feasibility through the pivot; \(J=\varnothing\) certifies primal infeasibility for the selected row.

notation.meaning: Selected tableau row over nonbasic columns.
Sign associated with the active bound of nonbasic variable j.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The bounded-variable dual ratio test depends critically on objective, reduced-cost, tableau-row, and bound-orientation conventions. No source supports the displayed eligibility signs, ratio, or the claimed infeasibility certificate, so the exact variant cannot be validated reliably.

knowledge_statements.title: Numerically Guarded Ratio Tests
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Tolerance-aware primal ratio test with a deterministic stability-oriented tie break.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given primal-feasible \(x_B\), oriented direction \(g=\sigma B^{-1}a_q\), feasibility tolerance \(\varepsilon_f\geq0\), and pivot tolerance \(\varepsilon_p>0\), discard indices with \(|g_i|\leq\varepsilon_p\). For \(g_i>\varepsilon_p\), set \(r_i=(x_{B_i}-l_{B_i}+\varepsilon_f)/g_i\); for \(g_i<-\varepsilon_p\), set \(r_i=(u_{B_i}-x_{B_i}+\varepsilon_f)/(-g_i)\). Let \(r_{\min}=\min_i r_i\), retain candidates satisfying \(r_i\leq r_{\min}+\varepsilon_f/\max(|g_i|,\varepsilon_p)\), and choose among them an index with largest \(|g_i|\), breaking remaining ties deterministically. Recheck the accepted step against original bounds before updating the basis.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A guarded ratio test ignores tiny pivots, allows controlled feasibility tolerance, favors a stable pivot among near ties, and rechecks the step.
assumptions_latex: \(x_B\) is feasible within the declared tolerance.
\(\varepsilon_f\geq0\) and \(\varepsilon_p>0\) are fixed for the test.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The rule selects a numerically acceptable blocking row or reports that no pivot exceeds \(\varepsilon_p\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Ignoring small pivots and using a stability-oriented tie break fit this algorithmic container, but the specific tolerance-inflated ratios and candidate window are solver-dependent and uncited. A numerical-simplex source or explicit documented solver policy is required.

knowledge_statements.title: Single-Column Basis Exchange
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Rank-one algebra for replacing one basis column during a simplex pivot.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(B=[b_1,\ldots,b_m]\) be nonsingular, let column \(a_q\) enter, and let position \(p\) leave. With \(d=B^{-1}a_q\) and unit vector \(e_p\), the exchanged basis is \(B'=B+(a_q-b_p)e_p^{\mathsf T}=BE\), where \(E=I+(d-e_p)e_p^{\mathsf T}\). The exchange is valid exactly when \(d_p\neq0\); then \(E\) and \(B'\) are nonsingular and \(B'^{-1}=E^{-1}B^{-1}\), with \(E^{-1}=I-(d-e_p)e_p^{\mathsf T}/d_p\). Thus one simplex pivot is a rank-one basis modification.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Replacing one basis column is a rank-one update; it produces a valid basis exactly when the pivot component is nonzero.
assumptions_latex: \(B\in\mathbb R^{m\times m}\) is nonsingular.
The entering column \(a_q\in\mathbb R^m\) and leaving position \(p\) are specified.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(B'\) is nonsingular if and only if \(d_p\neq0\), and its inverse has the displayed rank-one update.

notation.meaning: Entering column expressed in basis coordinates.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The rank-one column-replacement identities and nonsingularity condition are mathematically consistent, and representation is an appropriate knowledge kind, but no source with an inspectable locator is supplied.

knowledge_statements.title: Bound-Flip Transitions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bounded-variable simplex move that changes a nonbasic active bound without exchanging basis columns.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let nonbasic variable \(x_q\) currently equal its lower bound \(l_q\), have finite upper bound \(u_q\), and move toward that upper bound along \(x_q(\theta)=l_q+\theta\). With \(d=B^{-1}a_q\), basic values satisfy \(x_B(\theta)=x_B-	heta d\). Compute the basic blocking step \(\theta_B\) by the primal ratio test. If \(u_q-l_q<\theta_B\), take \(\theta=u_q-l_q\), set \(x_q=u_q\), update \(x_B\), and reverse the bound status and reduced-cost eligibility of \(q\), while leaving \(B\) unchanged. The upper-to-lower case is obtained by reversing the direction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If an entering bounded variable reaches its opposite bound before any basic variable blocks, flip its bound status and retain the same basis.
assumptions_latex: \(B\) is nonsingular and the current solution is primal feasible.
Both bounds of \(x_q\) are finite and distinct.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: When \(u_q-l_q<\theta_B\), the transition preserves primal feasibility and changes no basis column.

notation.meaning: Basic displacement per unit increase of the flipping variable.
First step at which a basic variable reaches a bound.
Nonbasic variable undergoing the bound flip.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The described bound flip is mathematically plausible and appropriately classified as an algorithm, but it has no supporting citation. A bounded-variable simplex source must support the no-basis-exchange transition and status update.

knowledge_statements.title: Multi-Column Basis Exchange
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Block algebra for simultaneously replacing several columns of a nonsingular basis.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(B\in\mathbb R^{m\times m}\) be nonsingular, let \(P=(p_1,\ldots,p_r)\) be distinct basis positions, and let \(Q=[a_{q_1},\ldots,a_{q_r}]\) be entering columns. Define \(U=[e_{p_1},\ldots,e_{p_r}]\), \(B_P=BU\), and \(B'=B+(Q-B_P)U^{\mathsf T}=BM\), where \(M=I+(B^{-1}Q-U)U^{\mathsf T}\). The block exchange is valid exactly when the pivot block \(U^{\mathsf T}B^{-1}Q\) is nonsingular. In that case \(B'^{-1}=M^{-1}B^{-1}\), and \(M^{-1}\) may be evaluated by a rank-\(r\) Woodbury update.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Simultaneous replacement of several basis columns is valid precisely when the corresponding block pivot matrix is nonsingular.
assumptions_latex: \(B\) is nonsingular.
The positions in \(P\) are distinct and \(Q\) has the same number of columns.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(B'\) is nonsingular if and only if \(U^{\mathsf T}B^{-1}Q\) is nonsingular.

notation.meaning: Selector matrix for replaced basis positions.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The block column-replacement formula and pivot-block nonsingularity condition are internally consistent, and representation fits the leaf, but no source with a relevant locator is provided.

knowledge_statements.title: Basis Warm Starts
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Initialization of simplex on a modified LP from a previously available basis state.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given modified data \((A',b',c',l',u')\) and an index set \(\mathcal B\) inherited from a related solved linear program, form \(B'=A'_{\mathcal B}\). If \(|\mathcal B|=m\) and \(B'\) is nonsingular, assign each nonbasic variable to a permitted bound, compute \(x_{\mathcal B}=B'^{-1}(b'-A'_{\mathcal N}x_{\mathcal N})\), solve \(B'^{\mathsf T}y=c'_{\mathcal B}\), and compute \(\bar c_{\mathcal N}=c'_{\mathcal N}-A'_{\mathcal N}{}^{\mathsf T}y\). Start primal simplex if primal feasibility holds, dual simplex if dual feasibility holds, and otherwise invoke basis repair or Phase I. Output the initialized basis state and feasibility classification.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A warm start rebuilds primal and dual basis data under modified LP coefficients, then selects primal simplex, dual simplex, or repair according to feasibility.
assumptions_latex: The modified model has \(m\) equality rows and explicit variable bounds.
The inherited basis indices identify columns still present in \(A'\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The procedure either supplies a classified nonsingular basis state or routes the model to repair or Phase I.

notation.meaning: Reduced costs for the modified model.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The warm-start workflow fits the algorithm container, but no source supports the procedure. The meaning of dual feasibility also requires explicit objective and active-bound reduced-cost sign conventions.

knowledge_statements.title: Post-Modification Basis Repair
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Recovery of a usable simplex basis after rows, columns, bounds, or coefficients change.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given modified LP data and a prior basic index set \(\mathcal B\), delete indices of removed columns, incorporate mandatory new rows, and test the candidate matrix \(A'_{\mathcal B}\) for dimension \(m\), numerical rank \(m\), and acceptable conditioning. If deficient, add linearly independent structural or auxiliary columns until a nonsingular basis \(B'\) is obtained. Assign nonbasic variables to admissible bounds, recompute basic values and reduced costs, and classify primal and dual feasibility. Apply primal pivots, dual pivots, or Phase I until a feasible basis state is recovered or infeasibility is certified. Output the repaired basis, or the resulting certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: After model changes, repair removes invalid basis columns, restores rank, recomputes basis state, and pivots or runs Phase I until recovery or certification.
assumptions_latex: The modified linear program is represented in equality form with bounds.
Auxiliary columns may be introduced when structural columns cannot complete a basis.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The procedure returns a nonsingular classified basis state or a valid infeasibility outcome.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Basis repair is solver-dependent, and no citation supports the proposed column-completion, conditioning, pivot, and Phase-I policy. The claim that the procedure necessarily reaches recovery or a valid certificate also requires stated termination and certification conditions.

knowledge_statements.title: Interior-Point Crossover Basis Interface
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conversion of an approximate interior-point solution into a simplex basic solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given LP data \((A,b,c,l,u)\) and an approximate primal-dual point \((x,y,z^l,z^u)\), classify variables near a bound using declared primal and complementarity tolerances. Select \(m\) remaining columns whose matrix \(B=A_{\mathcal B}\) is numerically nonsingular, assigning all other variables to selected bounds. Compute \(x_{\mathcal B}=B^{-1}(b-A_{\mathcal N}x_{\mathcal N})\), \(B^{\mathsf T}\hat y=c_{\mathcal B}\), and \(\bar c_{\mathcal N}=c_{\mathcal N}-A_{\mathcal N}^{\mathsf T}\hat y\). Use primal or dual simplex cleanup when one feasibility system holds; otherwise perform basis repair or Phase I. Output a basic feasible optimal solution when cleanup terminates optimally.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Crossover selects a nonsingular basis from an interior-point estimate, reconstructs exact basis quantities, and uses simplex cleanup to obtain a basic optimum.
assumptions_latex: The equality-form LP has row rank \(m\).
The supplied primal-dual point satisfies the declared approximation tolerances.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Successful crossover returns a simplex basis state and, after optimal cleanup, a basic optimal solution.

notation.meaning: Columns selected for the crossover basis.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The supplied inventory concerns interior-point methods generally and does not locate a crossover algorithm. The assumptions do not establish that m columns outside the near-bound classification form a numerically nonsingular basis, so an authoritative crossover source is needed to determine the correct selection and cleanup conditions.

children.title: Basis Factorization-Update Family
children.top_down_role: Representations and maintenance strategies for repeated basis solves, including sparse execution and numerical reliability.

top_down_textbook_witnesses.source: Towards a Practical Parallelisation of the Simplex Method
top_down_textbook_witnesses.locator: Serial revised-simplex techniques and computational components
top_down_textbook_witnesses.source_title: Towards a Practical Parallelisation of the Simplex Method

knowledge_statements.title: Explicit Basis Inverse
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dense inverse representation of the linear solves associated with a simplex basis.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a nonsingular simplex basis \(B\in\mathbb R^{m\times m}\), the explicit-inverse representation stores \(H=B^{-1}\). Every primal basis solve and transposed dual solve are then represented by \(Bx=r\iff x=Hr\) and \(B^{\mathsf T}y=s\iff y=H^{\mathsf T}s\). After replacing basis column \(p\) by \(a_q\), let \(d=Ha_q\). If \(d_p\neq0\), update \(H\) by \(H'=[I-(d-e_p)e_p^{\mathsf T}/d_p]H\). In finite precision, accumulated update error can make \(H'B'\neq I\), so residual monitoring and periodic refactorization are required for numerical reliability.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An explicit basis inverse turns basis solves into matrix products and admits rank-one pivot updates, but finite-precision error requires residual checks and refactorization.
assumptions_latex: \(B\) is nonsingular.
For an exchange update, the pivot component satisfies \(d_p\neq0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(H=B^{-1}\) represents both basis-solve orientations, and the displayed formula represents a valid single-column exchange update.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The explicit-inverse representation and rank-one update are algebraically consistent and appropriately classified as a representation. No citation supports either the formulas or the finite-precision recommendation concerning residual monitoring and periodic refactorization.

knowledge_statements.title: Product-Form Inverse
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Product representation of inverse basis changes under successive simplex column replacements.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(m\in\mathbb N\), let \(B_0\in\mathbb R^{m\times m}\) be nonsingular, and let \(k\in\mathbb N\). For each \(j=1,\ldots,k\), choose \(r_j\in\{1,\ldots,m\}\) and \(a_j\in\mathbb R^m\), obtain \(B_j\) from \(B_{j-1}\) by replacing column \(r_j\) with \(a_j\), set \(d_j=B_{j-1}^{-1}a_j\), and define \(E_j=I+(d_j-e_{r_j})e_{r_j}^{T}\). Then \(B_j=B_{j-1}E_j\). If \((d_j)_{r_j}\ne0\), then \(E_j^{-1}=I-(d_j-e_{r_j})e_{r_j}^{T}/(d_j)_{r_j}\), and \[B_k^{-1}=E_k^{-1}E_{k-1}^{-1}\cdots E_1^{-1}B_0^{-1}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For each of k column replacements, the new basis equals the preceding basis times an invertible eta matrix. Consequently, the current inverse is the initial inverse preceded by the inverse eta matrices in reverse update order.
assumptions_latex: \(m,k\in\mathbb N\).

knowledge_statements.title: Eta-File Representation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sparse storage and application of product-form inverse update factors.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(m\in\mathbb N\), let \(B\in\mathbb R^{m\times m}\) be nonsingular, let \(a\in\mathbb R^m\), and let \(r\in\{1,\ldots,m\}\). Set \(d=B^{-1}a\) and suppose \(d_r\ne0\). The inverse eta matrix \(H=E^{-1}\), where \(E=I+(d-e_r)e_r^T\), differs from the identity only in column \(r\): \[H_{rr}=d_r^{-1},\qquad H_{ir}=-d_i/d_r\quad\text{for }i\ne r.\] An eta-file stores \(r\), \(d_r^{-1}\), and the indexed nonzero values \(-d_i/d_r\). For a sequence \(H_1,\ldots,H_k\), applying \(B_0^{-1}\) first and then applying \(H_1,\ldots,H_k\) chronologically realizes \(H_k\cdots H_1B_0^{-1}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An eta file stores only the changed column of each inverse update. After applying the initial inverse, applying the stored transformations in chronological order realizes their required product.

The transformed pivot satisfies \(d_r\ne0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The stored entries determine \(H=I-(d-e_r)e_r^T/d_r\) exactly in exact arithmetic.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Sparse LU update after a simplex basis exchange
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Forrest–Tomlin-style factor updating, its stability–sparsity boundary, and the condition motivating periodic refactorization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Suppose $B=LU$ and a simplex pivot replaces basis column $p$ by $A_q$, producing $B^+$. Let $P_1$ cyclically move position $p$ to position $m$ in both rows and columns. Sparse Gaussian elimination yields lower- and upper-triangular matrices $L_1,U_1$ such that
\[
P_1L^{-1}B^+P_1^T=L_1U_1,
\]
where $L_1$ differs from the identity only in its last row. Hence
\[
B^+=L^+U^+,
\qquad L^+=LP_1^TL_1,
\qquad U^+=U_1P_1.
\]
The permutation and sparse update factors may be stored implicitly and applied through permutations and sparse triangular substitutions. Large update multipliers can cause numerical instability; stabilizing row exchanges can bound such multipliers but may increase fill. Because accumulated updates increase storage, solve time, and possibly numerical error, simplex implementations periodically discard them and compute a fresh sparse LU factorization.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: After one simplex basis column is exchanged, a cyclic row-and-column permutation moves the loss of triangularity to the last row, where sparse elimination produces compact update factors. These factors give an implicit LU factorization of the new basis and can be stored rather than assembled. Large multipliers signal possible instability; row swaps improve stability at the cost of denser factors. Accumulated storage, solve cost, and error therefore motivate periodic fresh factorization.
assumptions_latex: B=LU\text{ is the current nonsingular basis factorization}
B^+\text{ is obtained from }B\text{ by replacing basis column }p\text{ with }A_q
P_1\text{ cyclically moves index }p\text{ to }m\text{ in rows and columns}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: P_1L^{-1}B^+P_1^T=L_1U_1\implies B^+=(LP_1^TL_1)(U_1P_1),\quad\text{with compact implicit updates and periodic refactorization required when update accumulation or instability becomes excessive.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Sparse LU realization of simplex basis solves
knowledge_statements.scope_note: LU-based solution of simplex basis systems and maintenance of sparse factors across one-column basis changes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let the nonsingular simplex basis matrix satisfy \(B=LU\), where \(L\) is unit lower triangular and \(U\) is upper triangular, with any row and column permutations incorporated into \(B\). The systems
\[
B^T\lambda=c_{\mathrm B},\qquad Bd=A_q
\]
are solved using the factors rather than by explicitly forming \(B^{-1}\). In particular, the primal basis solve is performed by
\[
L\bar d=A_q,\qquad Ud=\bar d.
\]
The transposed system is likewise recovered by triangular substitutions involving the transposed factors. Because consecutive simplex bases differ by one column, updating a maintained factorization is less expensive than recomputing it at every iteration. Sparse row and column permutations are chosen to balance numerical stability, sparsity of the factors, and useful triangular structure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonsingular simplex basis is factored as a sparse LU product, and the primal and transposed basis systems are solved through triangular substitutions rather than by forming the inverse. Since a simplex pivot changes only one basis column, maintaining the factors is cheaper than refactoring at every iteration. Pivoting and reordering must balance numerical stability, sparsity, and structural efficiency.
assumptions_latex: B\in\mathbb R^{m\times m}\text{ is a nonsingular simplex basis matrix}
B=LU
L\text{ is unit lower triangular and }U\text{ is upper triangular}
\text{Any row and column permutations used in the factorization are incorporated into }B
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: L\bar d=A_q,\quad Ud=\bar d,\quad B^T\lambda=c_{\mathrm B}\text{ is solved through transposed triangular factors, and the sparse LU factors may be maintained across one-column basis changes.}

It predicts possible fill; numerical cancellation may make an entry structurally present but numerically zero.

children.title: Factorization Pivot Selection

knowledge_statements.title: Factorization Pivot Selection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Threshold Markowitz pivot selection for an active sparse LU submatrix.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given an active matrix \(A^{(k)}\) and threshold \(u\in(0,1]\), form \[C_k(u)=\{(i,j):a_{ij}^{(k)}\ne0,\ |a_{ij}^{(k)}|\ge u\max_\ell|a_{\ell j}^{(k)}|\}.\] For each candidate, let \(r_i\) and \(c_j\) be the active structural nonzero counts in row \(i\) and column \(j\). Choose a candidate minimizing the Markowitz count \((r_i-1)(c_j-1)\), break ties by larger \(|a_{ij}^{(k)}|\), interchange it into the next pivot position, and continue until the active matrix is exhausted or \(C_k(u)\) is empty.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choose a threshold-acceptable pivot that minimizes predicted one-step fill, preferring the larger magnitude when fill scores tie.
assumptions_latex: \(A^{(k)}\) is the current active submatrix.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The selected pivot minimizes \((r_i-1)(c_j-1)\) over \(C_k(u)\), subject to the stated tie rule.

notation.meaning: active row and column nonzero counts

children.title: Factorization Stability Regimes

knowledge_statements.title: Factorization Stability Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Operational classification using element growth and normwise backward error.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For computed factors and permutations satisfying \(PBQ\approx LU\), define \(\rho=\max_{i,j,k}|a_{ij}^{(k)}|/\max_{i,j}|b_{ij}|\) and \(\eta=\|PBQ-LU\|_\infty/(\|B\|_\infty+\|L\|_\infty\|U\|_\infty)\). Given tolerances \(\rho_{\max}\ge1\) and \(\tau>0\), call the factorization stable when \(\rho\le\rho_{\max}\) and \(\eta\le\tau\), marginal when exactly one inequality fails, and unstable when both fail. A singular or rejected pivot places the factorization in the unstable regime independently of these ratios.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Growth and backward error jointly classify a factorization as stable, marginal, or unstable; pivot breakdown is always unstable.
assumptions_latex: \(B\ne0\) and finite computed factors \(L,U\) are available.
Positive acceptance tolerances are fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed predicates partition completed non-breakdown factorizations into stable, marginal, and unstable regimes.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: growth and backward error are standard numerical stability diagnostics

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The matrices underlying \(a_{ij}^{(k)}\) are not introduced, and the stable/marginal/unstable partition is an implementation-defined classification rather than a standard theorem. Its precise diagnostics and thresholds require a source.

children.title: Sparsity–Stability Tradeoff

knowledge_statements.title: Sparsity–Stability Tradeoff
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Monotonic tradeoff induced by threshold-constrained Markowitz pivoting.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a fixed active matrix, define \(C(u)=\{(i,j):a_{ij}\ne0,\ |a_{ij}|\ge u\max_\ell|a_{\ell j}|\}\) and \(M(u)=\min_{(i,j)\in C(u)}(r_i-1)(c_j-1)\), with \(M(u)=+\infty\) if \(C(u)=\varnothing\). If \(0<u_1\le u_2\le1\), then \(C(u_2)\subseteq C(u_1)\) and hence \(M(u_1)\le M(u_2)\). Thus strengthening the magnitude threshold can exclude low-fill pivots; weakening it enlarges sparse choices but permits smaller pivots.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A stricter pivot threshold improves magnitude screening but can only worsen the best available Markowitz fill score.
assumptions_latex: The active matrix and structural counts are fixed while thresholds are compared.
Column-threshold Markowitz selection is used.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(u_1\le u_2\) implies \(C(u_2)\subseteq C(u_1)\) and \(M(u_1)\le M(u_2)\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: the monotonicity follows directly from threshold candidate-set inclusion

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The candidate-set inclusion and Markowitz-score monotonicity are mathematically correct for a fixed active matrix, but no inspectable published locator is supplied.

knowledge_statements.title: Fill-Reducing Ordering
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Greedy symbolic ordering based on predicted one-step LU fill.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a structural pattern \(S_0\) of an \(m\times m\) matrix. At step \(k\), among structurally admissible active pivots \((i,j)\), select one minimizing \((r_i-1)(c_j-1)\); append \(i\) and \(j\) to the row and column permutations, add every symbolic fill pair \((p,q)\) for which \((p,j)\) and \((i,q)\) are active, and remove pivot row \(i\) and column \(j\). Stop after \(m\) pivots or upon structural breakdown. Output the permutations and predicted factor pattern.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Repeatedly choose the structurally admissible pivot with least predicted local fill, update the symbolic graph, and return row and column orderings.
assumptions_latex: Only structural nonzero information is used.
A deterministic tie rule is fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The output permutations encode the greedy minimum-Markowitz symbolic elimination order.

knowledge_statements.title: Bump Management
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Isolation and numerical elimination of the unresolved sparse-factorization nucleus.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given an active sparse matrix, repeatedly remove structural singleton rows or columns, recording their forced pivots and permutations, until no singleton remains. Call the remaining active submatrix the bump. Factor the bump using threshold pivot selection; after each pivot, update its structural degrees and extract any newly created singleton rows or columns. Stop when the bump is empty, a pivot cannot be accepted, or a prescribed bump-size limit triggers a fallback factorization. Assemble all recorded permutations and elimination factors into \(PBQ=LU\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strip forced singleton pivots, factor the remaining bump with stable sparse pivots, and resume singleton extraction whenever elimination creates new ones.

Pivot thresholds and any bump-size limit are fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: On successful exhaustion of the bump, the recorded operations define factors satisfying \(PBQ=LU\) in exact arithmetic.

knowledge_statements.title: Bartels–Golub Updates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: LU basis update by spike insertion and immediate triangular restoration.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(PBQ=LU\), a leaving basis position \(r\), and entering column \(a\), compute \(w=L^{-1}Pa\) by triangular solution and replace the corresponding column of \(U\) by \(w\). Apply row and column interchanges that place the resulting spike in elimination order, then use Gaussian transformations to remove its subdiagonal entries. Incorporate those transformations and permutations into updated factors \(\widehat L,\widehat U,\widehat P,\widehat Q\). Reject the update if a required pivot fails its stability test; otherwise output factors satisfying \(\widehat P B'\widehat Q=\widehat L\widehat U\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Transform and insert the entering column into the upper factor, then eliminate the spike immediately to restore an LU factorization.
assumptions_latex: \(PBQ=LU\) is a nonsingular basis factorization.
The replacement basis \(B'\) is nonsingular.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: An accepted update returns triangular factors of the column-replaced basis \(B'\).

notation.meaning: entering column transformed through the lower factor

knowledge_statements.title: Forrest–Tomlin Updates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sparse basis update retaining most existing factors and storing localized transformations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a sparse factorization \(PBQ=LU\), leaving position \(r\), and entering column \(a\), solve \(Lw=Pa\) and insert \(w\) into the corresponding column of \(U\). Use cyclic row and column permutations to move the induced spike to a trailing position, eliminate the resulting localized triangularity defect, and store the new sparse elementary transformations separately from the unchanged portion of \(L\). Accept only stable nonzero pivots. The updated permutations, retained factors, and stored transformations must compose to the column-replaced basis \(B'\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Move the update spike to a localized trailing region and store sparse correction transformations while retaining most existing factors.
assumptions_latex: A valid sparse LU basis factorization is available.
The updated basis is nonsingular and every accepted update pivot passes its stability test.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The retained factors and sparse corrections represent an exact factorization of \(B'\) in exact arithmetic.

knowledge_statements.title: Sparse Product-Form Updates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sparse application of inverse eta factors after basis replacements.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(m\in\mathbb N\), let \(B,B_0\in\mathbb R^{m\times m}\) be nonsingular, and suppose \(B^{-1}=H_k\cdots H_1B_0^{-1}\) for some \(k\in\mathbb N_0\). Given \(a\in\mathbb R^m\) and \(r\in\{1,\ldots,m\}\), let \(B'\) be obtained from \(B\) by replacing column \(r\) with \(a\), and compute \(d=B^{-1}a\). If \(d_r=0\), reject the replacement. Otherwise define \(H_{k+1}=I-(d-e_r)e_r^T/d_r\), store only \(r\), \(d_r^{-1}\), and the indexed nonzero values \(-d_i/d_r\) for \(i\ne r\), and set \(B'^{-1}=H_{k+1}B^{-1}\). Applying each factor uses only the coordinates indexed by its stored nonidentity column entries.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a specified entering column and leaving position, compute the transformed column and reject a zero pivot. Otherwise append the nonidentity entries of the new inverse eta factor, which updates the represented inverse to that of the column-replaced basis.
assumptions_latex: \(m\in\mathbb N\), \(B,B_0\in\mathbb R^{m\times m}\) are nonsingular, and \(B^{-1}=H_k\cdots H_1B_0^{-1}\) for \(k\in\mathbb N_0\).
\(a\in\mathbb R^m\) and \(r\in\{1,\ldots,m\}\).
Sparse indexed-vector arithmetic preserves every retained nonzero.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For \(d_r\ne0\), the augmented file represents \(B'^{-1}=H_{k+1}H_k\cdots H_1B_0^{-1}\).

knowledge_statements.title: Update-Depth Refactorization Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic refactorization trigger based on accumulated basis-update depth.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(k\) be the number of accepted basis updates since the last fresh factorization and let \(K_{\max}\in\mathbb N\) be a prescribed update-depth limit. Continue solving with the update representation while \(k<K_{\max}\). Immediately after an accepted update makes \(k\ge K_{\max}\), discard the accumulated update factors, compute a fresh factorization \(PBQ=LU\) of the current basis, and reset \(k=0\). A failed refactorization terminates this regime with a numerical-failure status rather than retaining the stale update chain.

knowledge_statements.title: Sparsity-Loss Refactorization Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A threshold policy for replacing accumulated basis updates after excessive fill-in.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(B_k\) be the current simplex basis, represented by factors of a reference basis together with accumulated updates. Let \(s_k\) denote the stored nonzero count of this representation, and let \(s_k^{\mathrm{ref}}>0\) estimate the nonzero count of freshly computed factors of \(B_k\). Given \(\tau_s>1\), the sparsity-loss refactorization condition is \[s_k>\tau_s s_k^{\mathrm{ref}}.\] When this condition holds, discard the update chain and compute new sparse factors of \(B_k\); otherwise retain the current representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Refactorize the current basis when accumulated updates require substantially more stored nonzeros than estimated fresh factors.

The stored and fresh-factor nonzero counts use the same counting convention.
\(\tau_s>1\) is fixed by the implementation.

knowledge_statements.title: Stability-Driven Refactorization Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A numerical-reliability trigger for rebuilding the current basis factors.

knowledge_statements.title: Basis Conditioning
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Normwise sensitivity of a nonsingular simplex basis matrix.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(B\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times m}\) be nonsingular, and let \(\lVert\cdot\rVert\) be a subordinate matrix norm. Its normwise condition number is \[\kappa(B)=\lVert B\rVert\,\lVert B^{-1}\rVert.\] If \(b\neq 0\), \(Bx=b\), and the right-hand side is perturbed by \(\Delta b\), then the corresponding change \(\Delta x\), defined by \(B\Delta x=\Delta b\), satisfies \[\frac{\lVert\Delta x\rVert}{\lVert x\rVert}\leq \kappa(B)\frac{\lVert\Delta b\rVert}{\lVert b\rVert}.\] Large \(\kappa(B)\) therefore permits amplification of relative right-hand-side perturbations in a basis solve.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Basis conditioning is measured by the product of the basis norm and inverse-basis norm; it bounds the amplification of relative right-hand-side perturbations in a basis solve.
assumptions_latex: \(B\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times m}\) is nonsingular.
The matrix norm is subordinate to the vector norm.
\(b\neq 0\) and \(Bx=b\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\kappa(B)=\lVert B\rVert\lVert B^{-1}\rVert\geq 1\).

notation.meaning: Normwise condition number of the basis.

knowledge_statements.title: Factor Growth
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Element-growth measure for a computed basis factorization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose Gaussian elimination with pivoting computes \(PB=LU\) from a nonsingular basis matrix \(B=(b_{ij})\). Let \(a_{ij}^{(t)}\) denote the active matrix entries after \(t\) elimination stages, with \(a_{ij}^{(0)}=b_{ij}\). The element-growth factor is \[\rho(B)=\frac{\max_{t,i,j}|a_{ij}^{(t)}|}{\max_{i,j}|b_{ij}|}.\] It measures the largest intermediate magnitude relative to the original basis entries; large \(\rho(B)\) can magnify floating-point backward error even when the factorization completes.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Factor growth is the largest magnitude produced during elimination divided by the largest original basis entry.
assumptions_latex: \(B\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times m}\) is nonsingular.

knowledge_statements.title: Conditioning–Growth Diagnostic
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A combined warning criterion for ill-conditioning and elimination growth.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\widehat{\kappa}(B)\) estimate the condition number of the current basis, let \(\widehat{\rho}(B)\) measure factor growth, and let \(u\) be unit roundoff. For a prescribed warning tolerance \(\tau\in(0,1)\), define \[D(B)=u\,\widehat{\kappa}(B)\,\widehat{\rho}(B).\] The conditioning–growth diagnostic raises a reliability warning when \(D(B)>\tau\). This criterion combines sensitivity of the exact basis equations with rounding-error amplification introduced by the computed factors; it is a conservative implementation diagnostic rather than an exact forward-error identity.

\(u>0\) is the arithmetic's unit roundoff.
\(\tau\in(0,1)\) is prescribed.

knowledge_statements.title: Basis Residual Monitoring
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Normwise residual tests for primal and transposed basis solves.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given computed solutions \(\widehat{x}\) and \(\widehat{y}\) to \(Bx=b\) and \(B^{T}y=c\), compute \[r_p=b-B\widehat{x},\qquad r_d=c-B^{T}\widehat{y},\] and the scaled residuals \[\eta_p=\frac{\lVert r_p\rVert}{\lVert B\rVert\lVert\widehat{x}\rVert+\lVert b\rVert},\qquad \eta_d=\frac{\lVert r_d\rVert}{\lVert B^{T}\rVert\lVert\widehat{y}\rVert+\lVert c\rVert}.\] Accept both solves if \(\max\{\eta_p,\eta_d\}\leq\tau_r\); otherwise request refinement or refactorization. A zero denominator is assigned residual zero only when its numerator is also zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Compute consistently scaled residuals for basis and transposed-basis solves, accepting them only when both meet the prescribed tolerance.
assumptions_latex: \(B\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times m}\) is the current basis matrix.
Each matrix norm is subordinate to the vector norm used with its corresponding system.
\(\tau_r>0\) is prescribed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\max\{\eta_p,\eta_d\}\leq\tau_r\Rightarrow\) accept the monitored solves.

source_refs.locator: Linear Algebra Issues p. 16

source_witnesses.locator: Linear Algebra Issues p. 16

knowledge_statements.title: Iterative Refinement for Basis Solves
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Residual-correction refinement using the maintained basis factors.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(B\), \(b\), an initial computed solution \(x^{(0)}\), a tolerance \(\tau_r>0\), and a correction limit \(J\in\mathbb{N}\), repeat for \(j=0,\ldots,J\): compute \(r^{(j)}=b-Bx^{(j)}\) in residual precision and return \(x^{(j)}\) if \[\frac{\lVert r^{(j)}\rVert}{\lVert B\rVert\lVert x^{(j)}\rVert+\lVert b\rVert}\leq\tau_r.\] If the test fails and \(j<J\), solve \(Bd^{(j)}=r^{(j)}\) with the maintained factors and set \(x^{(j+1)}=x^{(j)}+d^{(j)}\). If the test also fails for \(j=J\), report refinement failure and request refactorization or higher precision.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Repeatedly solve for the current residual and add the correction, testing the initial iterate and every corrected iterate until the tolerance is met or J corrections have failed.
assumptions_latex: \(B\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times m}\) is intended to be nonsingular.
Residuals are evaluated at least as accurately as correction solves.
\(J\in\mathbb{N}\) and \(\tau_r>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Return the first \(x^{(j)}\), with \(0\leq j\leq J\), whose scaled residual is at most \(\tau_r\), or report failure after testing \(x^{(J)}\).

children.title: Singular Basis Detection
children.top_down_role: Recognition of basis states lacking a usable factorization.

knowledge_statements.title: Singular Basis Detection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact and factorization-based criteria for detecting a singular basis.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A square basis matrix \(B\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times m}\) is singular exactly when \[\operatorname{rank}(B)<m,\] equivalently when there exists \(z\neq0\) with \(Bz=0\). In exact-arithmetic Gaussian elimination, this is detected when no nonzero admissible pivot exists at some stage. In floating-point implementation, a zero-pivot declaration must use a stated numerical-zero rule; such a declaration certifies numerical detection by that rule, not exact singularity without further validation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A basis is singular exactly when it lacks full rank; elimination detects this when no nonzero pivot exists in exact arithmetic.
assumptions_latex: \(B\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times m}\).
Exact singularity and tolerance-based numerical detection are distinguished.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(B\text{ is singular}\Longleftrightarrow\operatorname{rank}(B)<m\Longleftrightarrow\ker(B)\neq\{0\}\).

notation.meaning: Null space of the basis matrix.

children.title: Nearly Singular Basis Detection
children.top_down_role: Recognition of basis states approaching numerical rank loss.

knowledge_statements.title: Nearly Singular Basis Detection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Tolerance-based identification of an ill-conditioned but nonsingular basis.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(B\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times m}\) be nonsingular, and let \(\widehat{r}(B)>0\) estimate its reciprocal condition number \(1/\kappa(B)\) in a fixed norm. Given \(\tau_c\in(0,1)\), declare the basis nearly singular when \[0<\widehat{r}(B)\leq\tau_c.\] If a condition estimate is defined by \(\widehat{\kappa}(B)=1/\widehat{r}(B)\), the same trigger can be written as \(\widehat{\kappa}(B)\geq1/\tau_c\). The declaration is numerical and tolerance-dependent; it does not assert that \(\det(B)=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Declare a nonsingular basis nearly singular when its estimated reciprocal condition number is no greater than a prescribed threshold; an exactly reciprocal condition estimate gives the corresponding inverse threshold.
assumptions_latex: \(B\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times m}\) is nonsingular.
The reciprocal-condition estimator and norm are fixed.
\(\tau_c\in(0,1)\) is prescribed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(0<\widehat{r}(B)\leq\tau_c\Rightarrow\) declare \(B\) nearly singular.

notation.meaning: Condition estimate defined as the reciprocal of the reciprocal-condition estimate when that convention is used.

children.title: Singular-Basis Repair
children.top_down_role: Basis replacement responses after confirmed singularity.

knowledge_statements.title: Singular-Basis Repair
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Combinatorial replacement of dependent basic columns by independent nonbasic columns.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\) with \(\operatorname{rank}(A)=m\) and a singular index set \(I\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}\) of size \(m\), initialize \(J\) as a maximal linearly independent subset of \(I\). Repeatedly select \(q\notin J\) such that \(A_q\notin\operatorname{span}\{A_j:j\in J\}\), and set \(J\leftarrow J\cup\{q\}\), until \(|J|=m\). Output \(J\) and freshly factorize \(A_J\). Full row rank guarantees that an eligible column exists at every incomplete step.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Keep a maximal independent subset of the failed basis, add independent nonbasic columns, and refactorize the resulting full-rank basis.
assumptions_latex: \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\) has rank \(m\).
The input index set \(I\) has cardinality \(m\) but \(A_I\) is singular.
Linear-independence tests follow a stated numerical tolerance in floating point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(|J|=m\) and \(\operatorname{rank}(A_J)=m\).

notation.meaning: Column j of the constraint matrix.

children.title: Near-Singularity Recovery
children.top_down_role: Preventive recovery responses for numerically fragile bases.

knowledge_statements.title: Near-Singularity Recovery
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Recovery workflow for a full-rank basis whose solves are numerically unreliable.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a basis \(B=A_I\) declared nearly singular, first recompute its factors using stable pivoting and estimate the scaled residual and reciprocal condition number. If the residual meets \(\tau_r\) and the reciprocal condition estimate exceeds \(\tau_c\), retain \(I\). Otherwise search for \(p\in I\) and \(q\notin I\) such that \(J=(I\setminus\{p\})\cup\{q\}\) has full rank and an improved reciprocal condition estimate. Accept the first \(J\) satisfying both tolerances; if none is found, report recovery failure rather than continue unreliable basis solves.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Refactorize and retest a nearly singular basis; if reliability remains poor, exchange a column for a better-conditioned full-rank basis.
assumptions_latex: \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\) has full row rank.
The current basis \(A_I\) is numerically near singular.
Residual and conditioning tolerances are prescribed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Return a basis satisfying the residual and conditioning tests, or explicitly report recovery failure.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No citation supports the particular refactor-test-exchange workflow, search order, or acceptance policy. These choices are not canonical enough to retain without an inspectable source.

knowledge_statements.title: Sparse Basis-Solve Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Execution regime where sparse triangular traversal is preferable to dense substitution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a factorized basis satisfy \(PB=LU\), and let \(R_L(b)\) and \(R_U(b)\) be the row-index sets reached during the forward and backward solves for right-hand side \(b\). The solve is in the sparse regime when the factors are stored sparsely and \[\operatorname{nnz}(L_{R_L,:})+\operatorname{nnz}(U_{R_U,:})<\tau_d m^2,\] for a prescribed \(\tau_d\in(0,1)\), while the reached sets are not small enough to invoke a separate hypersparse kernel. In this regime, traverse only stored entries incident to the reached sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Use sparse triangular solves when the factor entries reached by the right-hand side are substantially fewer than a dense solve would inspect.
assumptions_latex: \(B\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times m}\) has stored sparse triangular factors.
Reach sets are available or can be computed.
\(\tau_d\in(0,1)\) is prescribed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The solve inspects entries supported on \(R_L(b)\) and \(R_U(b)\), rather than all \(m^2\) matrix positions.

notation.meaning: Number of stored nonzeros in M.

assumptions_latex: \(B\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times m}\) is nonsingular and stored through sparse triangular factors and updates.
The solve is \(Bx=r\) or \(B^{\mathsf T}x=r\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(|V_r|\leq \eta m\) and \(|V_x|\leq \eta m\) for a prescribed \(\eta\ll1\).

notation.meaning: Indices reached from the right-hand-side support in the factor dependency graph.
Indices visited or made nonzero during the solve.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Operational condition for graph-pruned sparse triangular basis solves.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(B\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times m}\) be represented by sparse triangular factors, possibly followed by basis-update transformations. For a right-hand side \(r\), let \(V_r\) be the dependency-graph reach of \(\operatorname{supp}(r)\), and let \(V_x\) contain every index visited or made nonzero while solving \(Bx=r\) or \(B^{\mathsf T}x=r\). The solve is in the hypersparse regime at threshold \(\eta\in(0,1)\) when \(|V_r|\leq\eta m\) and \(|V_x|\leq\eta m\). An implementation may then restrict traversal and arithmetic to the reached subgraph while retaining the same algebraic solution as a full triangular solve.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A basis solve is hypersparse when the right-hand side reaches and activates only a prescribed small fraction of the factor graph.
knowledge_statements.title: Hypersparse Basis-Solve Regime

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The operational thresholds and reached-subgraph execution claim are specialized implementation assertions with no cited source. A dedicated sparse triangular-solve or simplex implementation source is required to establish the terminology and correctness conditions.

assumptions_latex: \(B\) is represented by factors whose numerical solves generate intermediate nonzeros.
\(f_{\mathrm{work}}>0\) counts intermediate and output entries processed during one solve.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\phi=f_{\mathrm{work}}/\max\{1,\operatorname{nnz}(r),\operatorname{nnz}(x)\}\geq\tau_{\mathrm{fill}}\).

notation.meaning: Number of entries processed in intermediate solve vectors.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Operational classification by intermediate fill rather than factorization fill alone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a basis solve \(Bx=r\) or \(B^{\mathsf T}x=r\), let \(f_{\mathrm{work}}\) count the intermediate and output vector entries processed across all triangular factors and update transformations. Define the work-fill amplification by \(\phi=f_{\mathrm{work}}/\max\{1,\operatorname{nnz}(r),\operatorname{nnz}(x)\}\). Given an implementation threshold \(\tau_{\mathrm{fill}}>1\), the solve is fill-dominated when \(\phi\geq\tau_{\mathrm{fill}}\). In this regime the arithmetic and memory traffic are governed principally by intermediate fill, even if \(r\) or the final solution \(x\) is sparse.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A basis solve is fill-dominated when intermediate vectors expand enough that their processing, rather than input or output sparsity, controls the work.
knowledge_statements.title: Fill-Dominated Basis-Solve Regime

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The proposed work-fill amplification ratio and threshold are implementation-defined rather than standard mathematical terminology. No source supports this exact classification or the claim that intermediate fill principally governs arithmetic and memory traffic.

assumptions_latex: \(B\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times m}\) is nonsingular.
Right-hand-side blocks \(R\) and \(S\) have \(k\geq1\) columns.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Y=B^{-1}R\), \(Z=B^{-\mathsf T}S\), with independently checkable residuals \(R-BY\) and \(S-B^{\mathsf T}Z\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Block interface exposing independent right-hand sides for parallel execution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A parallel basis-solve interface accepts a fixed nonsingular basis matrix \(B\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times m}\), a mode selecting \(B\) or \(B^{\mathsf T}\), and a block of right-hand sides. For \(R=[r_1,\ldots,r_k]\), it returns \(Y=[y_1,\ldots,y_k]\) satisfying \(BY=R\); for \(S=[s_1,\ldots,s_k]\), it returns \(Z=[z_1,\ldots,z_k]\) satisfying \(B^{\mathsf T}Z=S\). Columns may be scheduled concurrently because each column equation is independent. Correctness is exposed through the columnwise residuals \(R-BY\) or \(S-B^{\mathsf T}Z\), evaluated under a declared numerical tolerance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The interface solves several independent right-hand sides against one basis or its transpose and exposes columnwise residuals for verification.
knowledge_statements.title: Parallel Basis-Solve Interface

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The block equations and independence of their columns are mathematically sound, and representation is an appropriate knowledge kind for an interface leaf. However, the claimed parallel interface contract, scheduling interpretation, and residual exposure have no cited implementation or numerical-linear-algebra source.

children.top_down_role: Basis-state manifestations and implementation safeguards only; general convergence proofs, pivot-path complexity, and complete anti-cycling theory are owned by the simplex convergence chapter.

assumptions_latex: The linear program is \(\min\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax=b,\ x\geq0\}\) with \(\operatorname{rank}(A)=m\).
\(B=A_{\mathcal B}\) is a primal-feasible basis.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The basis is primal degenerate exactly when \(\min_{i\in\mathcal B}(B^{-1}b)_i=0\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(\min\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax=b,\ x\geq0\}\), where \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\) has rank \(m\). A basis \(\mathcal B\) with \(|\mathcal B|=m\) and nonsingular \(B=A_{\mathcal B}\) defines \(x_{\mathcal B}=B^{-1}b\) and \(x_{\mathcal N}=0\). If \(x_{\mathcal B}\geq0\), the basis is primal degenerate when at least one basic variable is at its lower bound, equivalently when \((x_{\mathcal B})_i=0\) for some \(i\in\mathcal B\). The associated basic feasible solution is then called degenerate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A primal-feasible basis is degenerate when at least one of its basic variables equals zero.
knowledge_statements.title: Primal Basis Degeneracy

assumptions_latex: The problem is \(\min\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax=b,\ x\geq0\}\), where \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\) has rank \(m\).
\(B=A_{\mathcal B}\) is nonsingular and dual feasible, so \(\bar c_j\geq0\) for every \(j\in\mathcal N\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The basis is dual degenerate exactly when there exists \(j\in\mathcal N\) such that \(\bar c_j=0\).

notation.meaning: Simplex multiplier associated with the basis.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\min\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax=b,\ x\geq0\}\), where \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\) has rank \(m\), let \(\mathcal B\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}\) contain \(m\) indices, let \(B=A_{\mathcal B}\) be nonsingular, and set \(\mathcal N=\{1,\ldots,n\}\setminus\mathcal B\). Define \(y=B^{-\mathsf T}c_{\mathcal B}\) and \(\bar c_j=c_j-a_j^{\mathsf T}y\) for every \(j\in\mathcal N\). If \(\bar c_j\geq0\) for every \(j\in\mathcal N\), the basis is dual feasible. It is dual degenerate when \(\bar c_j=0\) for at least one \(j\in\mathcal N\); such a nonbasic column has zero first-order objective change per unit increase.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A dual-feasible basis is dual degenerate when at least one nonbasic variable has zero reduced cost.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mu(x)=|\{\mathcal B:A_{\mathcal B}^{-1}b=x_{\mathcal B},\ x_{\mathcal N}=0,\ x_{\mathcal B}\geq0\}|\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x\) be a basic feasible solution of \(Ax=b\), \(x\geq0\), with \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\) of rank \(m\). Define \(\mathfrak B(x)\) as the collection of index sets \(\mathcal B\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}\) such that \(|\mathcal B|=m\), \(A_{\mathcal B}\) is nonsingular, \(A_{\mathcal B}^{-1}b=x_{\mathcal B}\geq0\), and \(x_{\mathcal N}=0\). The basis multiplicity of \(x\) is \(\mu(x)=|\mathfrak B(x)|\). The point has multiple basis representations precisely when \(\mu(x)>1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Basis multiplicity counts the distinct nonsingular bases that represent the same basic feasible solution.

children.title: Zero-Length Pivot
children.top_down_role: Basis exchanges producing no primal movement.

assumptions_latex: \(B\) is a primal-feasible basis with \(x_{\mathcal B}=B^{-1}b\geq0\).
An entering column \(a_j\) has direction \(d=B^{-1}a_j\) with some \(d_i>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The pivot has zero length exactly when \(\theta^*=\min_{i:d_i>0}(x_{\mathcal B})_i/d_i=0\).

notation.meaning: Basic direction induced by the entering column.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(B\) be a primal-feasible basis, let \(x_{\mathcal B}=B^{-1}b\geq0\), and choose an entering nonbasic column \(a_j\). With \(d=B^{-1}a_j\), assume \(d_i>0\) for at least one \(i\). The primal ratio test gives \(\theta^*=\min_{i:d_i>0}(x_{\mathcal B})_i/d_i\). The pivot is zero-length when \(\theta^*=0\). The basis may change by replacing a minimizing basic index with \(j\), but the primal point remains unchanged because \(x_j\) increases by zero and \(x_{\mathcal B}\) changes by \(-\theta^*d=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A zero-length pivot changes the basis with ratio-test step zero, so the represented primal point does not move.

children.title: Multiplicity-Induced Pivot Stasis
children.top_down_role: Zero-movement behavior arising from alternative bases at one solution.

assumptions_latex: A feasible point \(x\) has distinct representing bases \(\mathcal B,\mathcal B'\in\mathfrak B(x)\).
A valid simplex exchange carries \(\mathcal B\) to \(\mathcal B'\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x'=x\) and \(c^{\mathsf T}x'=c^{\mathsf T}x\), although \(\mathcal B'\neq\mathcal B\).

notation.meaning: Basis before and after the exchange.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x\) be a degenerate basic feasible solution with \(\mu(x)>1\). Suppose distinct bases \(\mathcal B,\mathcal B'\in\mathfrak B(x)\) differ by a valid simplex exchange. Because both bases represent the same point, the corresponding pivot step is \(\theta^*=0\), the post-pivot point satisfies \(x'=x\), and the objective satisfies \(c^{\mathsf T}x'=c^{\mathsf T}x\). Thus basis multiplicity permits combinatorial motion through basis states without geometric or objective motion; repeated such exchanges produce pivot stasis until a positive-length pivot is selected.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Multiple bases of one degenerate point permit basis changes with zero step and no objective change.
knowledge_statements.title: Multiplicity-Induced Pivot Stasis

\(x^{(k)}\) is the basic feasible solution represented by \(\mathcal B_k\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A degenerate basis sequence satisfies \(\mathcal B_{k+1}\neq\mathcal B_k\) and \(x^{(k+1)}=x^{(k)}\) throughout the indexed run.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A finite or infinite simplex basis sequence \((\mathcal B_k)_{k\in K}\) is degenerate on an index run \(K'\subseteq K\) when every consecutive transition on that run changes the basis but has zero step. Equivalently, if \(x^{(k)}\) denotes the basic feasible solution represented by \(\mathcal B_k\), then \(\mathcal B_{k+1}\neq\mathcal B_k\) and \(x^{(k+1)}=x^{(k)}\) for every consecutive \(k,k+1\in K'\). Consequently, \(c^{\mathsf T}x^{(k)}\) is constant on the run even though the basis states may be distinct.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A degenerate basis sequence changes bases through consecutive zero-length pivots while leaving the represented feasible point fixed.
knowledge_statements.title: Degenerate Basis Sequences

assumptions_latex: A primal-simplex pivot uses entering reduced cost \(\bar c_j\) and feasible step \(\theta^*\geq0\).
The objective is \(c^{\mathsf T}x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(c^{\mathsf T}x'-c^{\mathsf T}x=\theta^*\bar c_j=0\) whenever \(\theta^*=0\) or \(\bar c_j=0\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a standard-form minimization problem, let a primal-simplex pivot introduce variable \(x_j\) with reduced cost \(\bar c_j\) and feasible step \(\theta^*\). If \(x'\) is the post-pivot point, then the exact objective change is \(c^{\mathsf T}x'-c^{\mathsf T}x=\theta^*\bar c_j\). Objective stalling occurs when this quantity is zero despite a basis change. In particular, every zero-length pivot with \(\theta^*=0\) stalls the objective; a positive-length pivot also stalls when \(\bar c_j=0\). A constant objective alone therefore does not imply that the basis state is unchanged.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Objective stalling occurs when a basis changes but the simplex objective change, equal to step times entering reduced cost, is zero.
knowledge_statements.title: Objective Stalling

assumptions_latex: The simplex implementation has a deterministic transition rule on complete basis states.
Each signature uniquely identifies the information determining the next transition.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A repeated signature \(\sigma_q=\sigma_p\) with \(p<q\) certifies a cycle of period \(q-p\).

notation.meaning: Canonical signature of the complete simplex state at iteration k.
Map from previously observed signatures to iteration indices.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact state-repetition detector for deterministic simplex transitions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a sequence of complete simplex states and a canonical signature \(\sigma_k\) containing the ordered basis, nonbasic bound statuses, and any deterministic tie-breaking state that affects the next pivot. Initialize an empty map \(H\). At iteration \(k\), compute \(\sigma_k\). If \(\sigma_k\notin H\), set \(H[\sigma_k]=k\) and continue. If \(\sigma_k\in H\), output \((p,k)=(H[\sigma_k],k)\) and stop. Under a deterministic transition rule, \(\sigma_k=sigma_p\) implies repetition of all subsequent states, so the segment from \(p\) through \(k-1\) is a detected basis cycle of period \(k-p\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Store complete deterministic simplex-state signatures; the first repeated signature detects and identifies a basis cycle.
knowledge_statements.title: Basis-Cycle Detection

children.title: Primal-Feasibility Tolerance Regime
children.top_down_role: Numerical acceptance regimes for primal feasibility.

assumptions_latex: \(B\) is the current computed basis matrix and \(\widehat x_{\mathcal B}\) is the computed basic solution.
\(\varepsilon_p,\varepsilon_r\geq0\) are declared primal and residual tolerances.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\min_i(\widehat x_{\mathcal B})_i\geq-\varepsilon_p\) and \(\|B\widehat x_{\mathcal B}-b\|_\infty\leq\varepsilon_r(1+\|b\|_\infty)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Absolute bound tolerance coupled with a scaled basis-equation residual test.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(B\widehat x_{\mathcal B}\approx b\) be a computed basic solution for a standard-form problem. Given tolerances \(\varepsilon_p\geq0\) and \(\varepsilon_r\geq0\), the basis is accepted as numerically primal feasible when \((\widehat x_{\mathcal B})_i\geq-\varepsilon_p\) for every basic index \(i\), and \(\|B\widehat x_{\mathcal B}-b\|_\infty\leq\varepsilon_r(1+\|b\|_\infty)\). Values in \([-varepsilon_p,0)\) are treated as tolerance-level bound violations rather than exact infeasibility. The chosen tolerances and scaling convention are part of the regime and must remain fixed when classifying a basis state.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A computed basis is treated as primal feasible when bound violations and the scaled basis-equation residual remain within declared tolerances.
knowledge_statements.title: Primal-Feasibility Tolerance Regime

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition is a plausible solver-specific feasibility regime, but the absolute bound tolerance, residual scaling, and requirement to combine both tests are conventions needing a numerical-optimization or solver source. The interval \([-varepsilon_p,0)\) also contains a malformed occurrence of \(\varepsilon_p\).

children.title: Dual-Optimality Tolerance Regime
children.top_down_role: Numerical acceptance regimes for reduced-cost optimality.

knowledge_statements.title: Dual-Optimality Tolerance Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Reduced-cost acceptance condition for a bounded-variable primal simplex basis state.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider the minimization problem \(\min\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax=b,\ l\le x\le u\}\). For a nonsingular basis matrix \(B=A_T\), compute \(y\) from \(B^{\mathsf T}y=c_T\) and reduced costs \(\bar c=c-A^{\mathsf T}y\). Given \(\varepsilon_d\ge0\), the basis state is dual-optimal within tolerance when \[|\bar c_i|\le\varepsilon_d\quad(i\in T),\qquad \bar c_j\ge-\varepsilon_d\quad(j\in L),\qquad \bar c_j\le\varepsilon_d\quad(j\in U),\] where nonbasic variables indexed by \(L\) and \(U\) are fixed at their lower and upper bounds, respectively.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A basis passes the dual test when basic reduced costs are nearly zero and each nonbasic reduced cost has the sign required by its active bound, within the dual tolerance.
assumptions_latex: \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) has rank \(m\).
\(T,L,U\) form the current bounded-variable basis partition.
\(B=A_T\) is nonsingular and \(\varepsilon_d\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\max\{\|\bar c_T\|_\infty,\ \max_{j\in L}(-\bar c_j)_+,\ \max_{j\in U}(\bar c_j)_+\}\le\varepsilon_d\).

notation.meaning: basic, lower-bound nonbasic, and upper-bound nonbasic index sets
positive part, equal to max of t and zero

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: bounded-variable reduced-cost sign conditions are standard, but tolerance scaling conventions vary

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition is mathematically coherent and the content kind fits the leaf, but the absolute reduced-cost tolerance convention is implementation-dependent and no inspectable source is cited.

children.title: Tolerance-Interaction Regime
children.top_down_role: Solver-state consequences of jointly selected feasibility plus optimality thresholds.

knowledge_statements.title: Tolerance-Interaction Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Joint primal and dual acceptance rule for a bounded-variable simplex state.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\min\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax=b,\ l\le x\le u\}\), let \((T,L,U)\) be a basis partition, set \(x_L=l_L\), \(x_U=u_U\), and solve \(B x_T=b-A_Ll_L-A_Uu_U\), where \(B=A_T\). Let \(v_p=\max\{\|Ax-b\|_\infty,\|(l-x)_+\|_\infty,\|(x-u)_+\|_\infty\}\), and let \(v_d\) be the maximum reduced-cost violation from the dual-tolerance condition. The state is accepted as approximately optimal exactly when \[v_p\le\varepsilon_p\quad\text{and}\quad v_d\le\varepsilon_d.\] Failure of either inequality must not be masked by enlarging only the other tolerance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Approximate optimality requires both primal and dual violations to meet their separate tolerances; passing one test cannot compensate for failing the other.
assumptions_latex: \(B=A_T\) is nonsingular.
\(0\le\varepsilon_p<\infty\) and \(0\le\varepsilon_d<\infty\).
Residuals and reduced costs use consistent scaling.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{accept}(T,L,U)\Longleftrightarrow(v_p\le\varepsilon_p\ \wedge\ v_d\le\varepsilon_d)\).

notation.meaning: maximum primal residual or bound violation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The joint condition fits the terminal container, but the exact acceptance equivalence, separate noncompensating tolerances, and consistent scaling requirement describe a solver policy for which no source is supplied.

knowledge_statements.title: Numerical Perturbation Safeguards
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Perturb-and-validate safeguard for degenerate or nearly tied simplex pivots.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(Ax=b\), objective \(c^{\mathsf T}x\), bounds \(l\le x\le u\), and tolerances \((\varepsilon_p,\varepsilon_d)\), choose perturbations \((\Delta b,\Delta c)\) with prescribed componentwise bounds and distinct lexicographic priorities. Apply simplex pivots to the perturbed data \((b+\Delta b,c+\Delta c)\), treating comparisons according to those priorities. After obtaining a candidate basis, discard the perturbations, recompute its primal solution and reduced costs from the original data, and accept it only if the original primal and dual tolerance tests pass. Otherwise reduce the perturbation scale or reject the basis; perturbed feasibility alone is never a certificate for the original problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Perturb data to resolve degeneracy, but validate every resulting basis against the unperturbed problem before accepting it.
assumptions_latex: The original linear program has finite input data.
Perturbation magnitudes and their priority order are fixed before affected comparisons.
Original-data residuals can be recomputed independently.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{output}=\text{candidate basis only if }v_p\le\varepsilon_p\text{ and }v_d\le\varepsilon_d\).

notation.meaning: original-data primal and dual violation measures
